<h2>A look around the world of open source</h2>

<p>What actually sustains an open source community when the cost of generating code drops toward zero, while the human labor required to review, govern, and secure it stays just as demanding? Across this week's reads, researchers, legal scholars, and builders examine the tension between automated volume and human stewardship—from public-infrastructure policy and maintainer bandwidth to provenance transparency, copyright law, and compact models running entirely on local hardware. Because software only serves people when human judgment remains in the loop, protecting maintainer agency and keeping project doors open to real newcomers matter more than ever.</p>

<h2>Shifting left in the AI coding era</h2>

<p>AI-powered velocity is transformative; however, it has silently introduced a potential reliability crisis by also increasing the velocity of “slop,” bugs, and session context collapse. Generative AI tools excel at increasing coding speed, but pure speed without structured guardrails means we are often auto-scaling our mistakes rather than simply writing code faster. We need a paradigm shift, aligning the human need for system comprehension with AI’s capacity for execution.</p>

<p>As co-author Dave Rensin outlines in the article <a href="https://drensin.medium.com/elephants-goldfish-and-the-new-golden-age-of-software-engineering-c33641a48874">Elephants, Goldfish, and the New Golden Age of Software Engineering</a>, “Design is the new code.”</p>

<h2>Understanding the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM)</h2>

<p>The EGM framework is a metaphor for a powerful way to develop AI-assisted software quickly and safely with humans intentionally in the loop.</p>

<p>The “Elephant” is a context-rich, long-horizon AI session that holds the end-to-end architectural vision and project memory. No code is written here; it is purely dedicated to design, intent, and capturing micro-decisions. The Elephant session is where the AI interviews you and you debate the merits of your choices.</p>

<p>Conversely, “Goldfish” are stateless, zero-context sessions used strictly to validate specifications. Because they share no “blind spots” with the designer, they act as objective critics, probing for gaps and edge cases.</p>

<p>The goal of this method is for the AI to correctly produce the code you wanted the first time after you press Enter.</p>

<h2>Announcing the open source Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin</h2>

<p>To put this methodology into practice at scale, we are thrilled to announce the <a href="https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model">Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin</a>. Originally, this plugin was developed internally for Google software engineers, and is now open source. Thousands of Googlers use this plugin every day to ship production Google code. Released under the Apache 2.0 license, the repository provides everything you need to implement this framework. Developers will find customizable Markdown rules, defined subagent personas, and structured review workflows ready to integrate into your own environments.</p>

<p>The plugin’s core goal is to bring the EGM framework directly into Antigravity, with other development environments upcoming. It automates the orchestration of the EGM lifecycle: managing context transfer between Elephants and Goldfish, facilitating validation loops, and rendering design documents, shifting the developer’s role from micromanager to executive reviewer.</p>

<h2>The EGM plugin in a nutshell</h2>

<figure class="wide borderless">
  <a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg34Cs37Wi55XbkPIhTo8U1vxrZ1PIbL7SSmo6hWb2bFy8pWfGAAtT0cOQXMlahzVmOTaPrpNOxsYqkbO_WU2nV1NrV77malOkK5Xusa_PbJdjBL3lAAQXcf3uLbn1-wmgNmHjB5ctLV0XChC8zQJ4QC6zrz1b7QnYVRJMwqEXS_aOtzTV9D1jr1WrZ7rM/s1600/image.png"><img alt="EGM lifecycle workflow diagram illustrating the three phases: Phase 1 Brainstorm (Growing the Elephant), Phase 2 Draft (Drafting with the Elephant), and Phase 3 Review (The Goldfish Protocol with Comprehension Check, Hostile Critic, and Implementation Readiness validators)." src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg34Cs37Wi55XbkPIhTo8U1vxrZ1PIbL7SSmo6hWb2bFy8pWfGAAtT0cOQXMlahzVmOTaPrpNOxsYqkbO_WU2nV1NrV77malOkK5Xusa_PbJdjBL3lAAQXcf3uLbn1-wmgNmHjB5ctLV0XChC8zQJ4QC6zrz1b7QnYVRJMwqEXS_aOtzTV9D1jr1WrZ7rM/s1600/image.png" /></a>
</figure>

<p>The EGM lifecycle, automated with the plugin, walks the user through three co-design phases:</p>

<h3>Phase 1: Growing the Elephant (<code class="inline">egm-brainstorm</code>)</h3>

<p>Developers load the system context and adhere to a “No Code” rule to co-design features, debate trade-offs, and challenge assumptions.</p>

<h3>Phase 2: Drafting with the Elephant (<code class="inline">egm-draft</code>)</h3>

<p>Developers iteratively draft a Markdown design document that covers the problem definition, technical plan, alternatives considered, and a detailed implementation plan that enumerates the specific files to change.</p>

<h3>Phase 3: The Goldfish Protocol (<code class="inline">egm-review</code>)</h3>

<p>The Goldfish Protocol shifts the model from co-design to adversarial validation, using stateless AI instances to probe the design for weaknesses. The plugin automates a three-step validation sequence:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Comprehension Check:</strong> A stateless Goldfish reads the complete design document and must explain the architecture and intent back to the Elephant. If the Goldfish cannot accurately summarize the plan, it indicates the document is ambiguous and requires further drafting.</li>
  <li><strong>Antagonistic Review:</strong> Multiple Goldfish instances assume the role of skeptical, antagonistic technical reviewers. They are tasked with identifying potential edge cases, hidden dependencies, and logical gaps. Their critique is funneled back to the Elephant session for resolution.</li>
  <li><strong>Implementation Readiness Check:</strong> A final Goldfish performs a strict go/no-go check. It verifies that all necessary information—file paths, data structures, and function signatures—is present and unambiguous. This ensures the spec is ready for precise transcription into code.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Human judgment is the artifact</h2>

<p>Ultimately, human judgment is the only artifact that truly matters in an AI-saturated world and we want to align the human need for system comprehension with AI’s capacity for execution. We hope this plugin will make it easier for developers of all skill levels to follow a process that more quickly and safely converts the idea they had in their head to a robust and well-built app on their screen.</p>

<p>We invite developers, architects, and AI enthusiasts to contribute to the plugin, customize its validation rules, and help define the future of collaborative software engineering.</p>

<p>While quantum computing holds the key to solving some of our most complex scientific challenges, current hardware is still limited by qubit counts and gate errors. Quantum error correction can overcome those errors, but it adds substantial overhead to every qubit and gate an algorithm uses. That makes circuit size one of the biggest factors in when a quantum algorithm becomes practical: every qubit and gate we remove lowers the bar that hardware must clear. To bring real-world quantum applications within reach sooner, it is critical to first compress the circuits that power them.</p>

<p>To help bridge this gap, the Google Quantum AI team is launching a <a href="https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation">competition on Kaggle</a> challenging you to use AI to build smaller, more efficient quantum circuits. The competition is powered by <a href="https://github.com/quantumlib/Qualtran/tree/main/kickmix">kickmix</a>, our new open source C++20 and Python library in <a href="https://github.com/quantumlib/Qualtran">Qualtran</a> for efficiently building and testing large quantum circuits. Our companion paper, <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23832">Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI</a>, describes the approach in detail.</p>

<h2>Turning compilation into an AI agent loop</h2>

<p>In the past, optimizing quantum algorithms meant domain experts meticulously tuning circuits by hand and publishing incremental wins one paper at a time. Today, agentic AI can search for more efficient circuits automatically, but such results can only be trusted when candidate circuits can be efficiently verified for correctness. For arbitrary quantum circuits, classical verification is intractable because quantum gates create superpositions over exponentially many classical bitstrings. Fortunately, many of the most expensive subroutines in fault-tolerant algorithms can be built within a structured subclass of circuits, called “kickmix” circuits, which we introduced in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/j3xf-bw18">our earlier work</a>. Built from reversible classical logic, diagonal phase gates, and measurement-based uncomputation, kickmix circuits map each input bitstring to a single output bitstring and phase without creating new superpositions. A classical computer can therefore run randomized fuzz testing on bitstring inputs in linear time to establish the circuit’s approximate correctness on full quantum states with high confidence.</p>

<p>Randomized fuzz testing does not prove exact equivalence, but most quantum algorithms can tolerate a small, bounded error. In fact, using approximations can cut gate and qubit counts significantly. Finding such approximations by hand is tedious, making it a great task for AI agents. With kickmix in Qualtran, agents can build large circuits quickly and fuzz test them at 60 billion gates per second on a single CPU core.</p>

<h2>How the competition works</h2>

<p>The competition features three benchmarks, each targeting a major kickmix bottleneck in a useful quantum algorithm in order to call attention to the broad utility of this verification paradigm. For each benchmark, we provide a reference baseline circuit and a standalone verifier, both open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Your goal is to submit a circuit that passes the verifier while minimizing a cost score based on its qubit and gate counts:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Fusion energy:</strong> Designing inertial confinement fusion targets requires simulating how quickly charged particles slow down in a hot, dense plasma fuel (<a href="https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2317772121">Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)</a>). The main bottleneck is computing the electric potential energy between every pair of particles, which is inversely proportional to their distance. The task is a quantum take on the classic fast inverse square root: given the squared distance <em>x</em>, apply a phase proportional to 1/&radic;<em>x</em>, accurate to a tiny fraction of its exact value.</li>
  <li><strong>Optimization:</strong> Decoded Quantum Interferometry (<a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09527-5">Nature</a>) is a quantum algorithm for solving hard combinatorial optimization problems. On one such problem, Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI), it finds better solutions than any known efficient classical algorithm. The main arithmetic bottleneck in solving OPI is decoding a Reed-Solomon code in superposition. The task is to build this decoder as a quantum circuit.</li>
  <li><strong>Chemistry:</strong> Fertilizer production depends on nitrogen fixation, which converts nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia. Industry does this at high temperature and pressure, using about 1&ndash;2% of the world’s energy supply, while bacteria do it at ambient conditions with the enzyme nitrogenase, whose active site is an iron-molybdenum cluster called FeMoCo. Understanding how FeMoCo works requires modeling its strongly correlated electrons, a long-standing target for quantum computers. Our recent algorithm (<a href="https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/pb2g-j9cw">Physical Review X (PRX)</a>) makes that quantum simulation cheaper by classically factorizing the molecule’s Hamiltonian into a compact sum of squares, so the quantum computer needs far fewer steps. At each step, the main bottleneck is a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.8.041015">quantum lookup table</a> that loads the parameters of that factorized Hamiltonian in superposition. The task is to co-design both parts: find an accurate factorization that needs fewer steps, and build compact circuits to load its parameters so each step costs less.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Get involved</h2>

<p>We have already seen the potential of AI-driven quantum research with <a href="https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/">Gemini 4 Argon</a>, which is helping researchers at Google accelerate progress across both quantum error correction and algorithm design. We’re excited that the broader research community is embracing this approach too, with <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22367">simultaneous independent work</a> pairing the kickmix paradigm with AI agents to reduce costs on related subroutines. However, our own internal runs with Gemini models show that all three benchmarks can be further improved beyond the circuits reported to date (and we’ve published a hash of those circuits in our recent manuscript to reveal after the competition), so the competition remains open and interesting.</p>

<p>Could we get more out of a quantum computer simply by asking it to do less? We invite you to help us answer that question.</p>

<h2>This Week in Open Source for October 15, 2026</h2>
<p><em>A look around the world of open source</em></p>

<p>After speaking about the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol and Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Toronto last week (<a href="https://fabricatedtechnobabble.com/a/3mxc6rqulrz23-tag-team-transmission-what-happened-when-we-brought-a2a-and-mcp-to-toronto">which I recapped in Tag-Team Transmission</a>), open agent boundaries were clearly still on my mind while collecting this week's reads. As AI agents, terminal tools, and embedded micro-apps move deeper into everyday software workflows, a central tension keeps surfacing across the open source community: where do human judgment, interface trust, and maintainer sustainability fit in? Whether teams are wiring up open protocols in the Unix shell, running multimodal retrieval locally on a laptop, or stewarding decades-old kernel infrastructure, the healthiest open source architectures don't replace human agency—they give workers clearer boundaries, inspectable tools, and a genuine seat at the controls.</p>

<p>Open source software is used pervasively, with some <a href="https://static.carahsoft.com/concrete/files/1617/1597/8665/2024_Open_Source_Security_and_Risk_Analysis_Report_WRAPPED.pdf">estimating</a> that over 90% of codebases contain open source software. Many adopt open source software because it’s free and thus cheaper than writing a proprietary alternative. But as the community saying goes: “open source is free as in puppies, not free as in beer.” Once you or your organization has adopted an open source project, there is still effort (such as engineering time, costs, etc.) associated with ensuring that your version of an open source project is healthy and up to date.</p>

<p>While efforts by the research community have investigated the ongoing costs required to <a href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/7816452"><em>maintain</em></a> open source software, at Google we needed to better understand the resources required to <em>use</em> <a href="https://opensource.googleblog.com/2024/08/2023-open-source-contribution-report.html">thousands</a> of open source software packages.</p>

<p>To better understand this cost, we designed a study to evaluate the effort (in software engineering hours) associated with maintaining open source software packages within Google. We focused on the following questions:</p>

<p><em>RQ1: How long does it take for an engineer (not a maintainer of the upstream project) to update an open source software package at Google?</em></p>

<p><em>RQ2: Can complexity metrics predict the relative effort/amount of time to update a package at Google?</em></p>

<h2>Customization incurs additional cost</h2>

<p>The majority of open source package updates (at Google) take four hours or less. However, the long tail could be days to months to fully land a package update. We needed to understand what makes the difference between hours, days, and months.</p>

<p>Our results suggested metrics that could be better predictors of update complexity than others. For example, local patches and customization, the number of package dependencies, and the number of upstream contributors, were better indicators of update complexity than the age of the package, or how many teams were using that package internally.</p>

</figure>

<h3>Study limitations and future work</h3>

<p>As this study was completed at Google, we acknowledge there are bias and limitations of our findings, including the following:</p>

<ul>
<li><strong>Business priority-based sampling:</strong> While rigorous, generalizable research studies thoroughly interrogate samples to minimize bias and maximize analytic potential, we designed this study to focus on existing data and minimize new data collection which could impact engineering roadmaps.</li>
<li><strong>We did not dictate tooling:</strong> We did not specify what tools (including genAI-enabled features) could or could not be used in the update process, and as such did not investigate the impact of any specific tool.</li>
<li><strong>Bias towards Go:</strong> Our collected data had significant bias towards Go. Given the lack of variety in our sample, we could not investigate the effect of language ecosystems, but other internal efforts indicated that language may significantly impact maintenance efforts. We encourage this line of investigation for future studies.</li>
<li><strong>Only active projects:</strong> This effort did not include significant data collection on stale or archived packages.</li>
</ul>

<img class="metadata" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjRNZHxQAbx9PNilxTAW04T1lLNqzvgxvVVWnCZHb0apsvl2EfEQ2DWmOkC0KFhduxTRZ9JRA_6pOPqGoiOvjiN_mNJOKrTZQxlzStCSnlj9N8yblR776WDuhOEjMvCnsPgowXUj-OC8iSYabkBDdwqtNjjzAE72eIF8xBZ5VZXpbEZbWGTJuFbYQcfS7M/s1600/incremental_rebuild_by_size_v5.png">

<p>Python is one of the primary languages at Google, powering everything from machine learning research to developer infrastructure and data pipelines. Across hundreds of thousands of files in our monorepo, fast and reliable static type checking is essential for maintaining code safety and developer velocity.</p>

<p>Today, <a href="https://pyrefly.org/"><strong>Pyrefly</strong></a>—an open source type checker developed by Meta—is the Python type checker at Google.</p>

<p>Replacing our previous type-checking infrastructure with Pyrefly provided significant speedups for engineers and agents alike, while substantially reducing build-system compute resources.</p>

<h2>Moving away from Pytype</h2>

<p>For more than a decade, Google relied on <a href="https://github.com/google/pytype"><strong>Pytype</strong></a>, an internally developed type checker that pioneered Python type checking and collaborated with the open source community to create <a href="https://github.com/python/typeshed">typeshed</a>.</p>

<p>However, as Python’s typing system evolved rapidly, Pytype faced fundamental challenges. Because it operated by analyzing compiled bytecode rather than source ASTs, keeping pace with modern typing PEPs became an increasing maintenance burden due to bytecode instability across Python releases. In addition, it struggled to deliver the fast turnaround times required for modern development loops.</p>

<p>As detailed in the <a href="https://github.com/google/pytype/blob/main/README.md">Pytype update</a>, we decided that Python 3.12 would be the final supported version for Pytype, leading us to evaluate and adopt modern open source alternatives.</p>

<h2>Why Pyrefly?</h2>

<p>Pyrefly incorporates years of collective lessons from earlier tools across the Python typing ecosystem. When evaluating candidates to succeed Pytype, Pyrefly quickly stood out across three key areas:</p>

<h3>Performance</h3>

<p>Written in Rust, Pyrefly is designed for high throughput and lazy, parallel evaluation. In our internal benchmarks across various Google projects, it proved to be an order of magnitude faster than Pytype, while scaling smoothly across large dependency graphs.</p>

<h3>Typing spec conformance</h3>

<p>Pyrefly achieves strong conformance—scoring roughly 97% on the official <a href="https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/python/typing/blob/main/conformance/results/results.html">typing conformance test suite</a>—and is actively maintained to track new Python versions and typing PEPs. This comprehensive language support makes Python version upgrades across our monorepo smoother.</p>

<p>In addition to supporting new syntax, Pyrefly provides strict type safety in areas where Pytype was historically permissive. A notable example is <strong>unsound unions</strong>: Pytype allowed passing a value of a union type (such as <code class="inline">int | None</code> or <code class="inline">int | str</code>) to a function expecting a specific type (such as <code class="inline">int</code>), as long as at least one type in the union was compatible. However, Pyrefly enforces sound union checking, catching these mismatches:</p>

<pre style="overflow-x: auto;"><code class="codebox python" style="white-space: pre-wrap; overflow-wrap: break-word;"># foo.py
def process_id(x: int) -&gt; None:
    ...
def get_id() -&gt; int | None:
    ...
val = get_id()
# Accepted by Pytype, but rejected by Pyrefly:
process_id(val)</code></pre>

<h3>Actionable error diagnostics</h3>

<p>Pyrefly provides Rust-style compiler diagnostics, displaying the offending code snippet with inline annotations that point directly to the root cause of type mismatches, sometimes with suggested fixes. E.g., for the <code class="inline">foo.py</code> example above, Pyrefly produces:</p>

<pre style="background: #f6f6f6; padding: 12px; font-size: 12px; line-height: 1.5; font-family: monospace; white-space: pre-wrap; overflow-wrap: break-word; word-break: break-word; overflow-x: auto; border-radius: 4px; box-sizing: border-box;"><span style="color: #c92a2a; font-weight: bold;">ERROR</span> Argument <span style="color: #0b7285;">`int | None`</span> is not assignable to parameter <span style="color: #0b7285;">`x`</span> with type <span style="color: #0b7285;">`int`</span> in function <span style="color: #0b7285;">`process_id`</span> <span style="color: #862e9c; font-weight: bold;">[bad-argument-type]</span>
 <span style="color: #1864ab; font-weight: bold;">--&gt;</span> foo.py:8:12
  <span style="color: #1864ab; font-weight: bold;">|</span>
<span style="color: #1864ab; font-weight: bold;">8 |</span> process_id(val)
  <span style="color: #1864ab; font-weight: bold;">|</span>            <span style="color: #c92a2a; font-weight: bold;">^^^</span>
  <span style="color: #1864ab; font-weight: bold;">|</span>
  The declared type does not allow <span style="color: #0b7285;">`None`</span>. Consider narrowing the value with an <span style="color: #0b7285;">`is not None`</span> check.</pre>

<h2>Performance and infrastructure impact</h2>

<p>Switching to Pyrefly brought measurable improvements across Google's developer ecosystem and infrastructure:</p>

<ul>
<li><strong>Up to 98% faster incremental rebuilds:</strong> In developer edit-and-rebuild workflows (with a warm daemon during active editing cycles), Pyrefly delivered up to a 98% latency reduction across various targets. On large machine learning targets, type-checking times dropped from minutes to seconds.</li>
<li><strong>&gt;90% critical-path reduction in clean builds:</strong> In cold-cache benchmark suites across major libraries and models, Pyrefly consistently reduced the type-checking share of the build critical path by 90% to 99%, eliminating a long-standing bottleneck in our build pipelines.</li>
<li><strong>&gt;80% compute hardware savings:</strong> Pyrefly reduced Google’s daily peak compute occupancy for Python type checking by more than 80%, saving thousands of machine cores every day.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Developer feedback</h2>

<p>Beyond aggregate metrics, Pyrefly improved the day-to-day development loop, allowing engineers and AI coding agents to catch bugs faster.</p>

<p>Here is what engineers across Google have shared about their experience:</p>

<blockquote><p><em>"I haven't waited for a Pytype action to complete since our project switched [to Pyrefly]. It is doubly awesome for agentic coding. Type checking is faster than running the tests now."</em> — <strong>Peter Hawkins</strong>, JAX Tech Lead</p></blockquote>

<blockquote><p><em>"I really like that Pyrefly gives super clear errors that point out exactly what's wrong."</em> — <strong>Yotam Doron</strong>, Gemini Large Scale Pretraining</p></blockquote>

<blockquote><p><em>“Investing in Python tooling pays huge dividends for research velocity: Pyrefly keeps our experimental iterations fast and catches subtle bugs early with clear, actionable errors.”</em> — <strong>Tom Ward</strong>, GDM Science</p></blockquote>

<h2>Looking forward</h2>

<p>Adopting Pyrefly highlights the value of uniting behind shared open source developer tooling. We are deeply grateful to the Pyrefly team for their rapid turnaround and responsiveness on upstream issues throughout our rollout. We look forward to continuing our collaboration and contributing to the Python open source community.</p>

<p>To learn more about Pyrefly or try it in your own projects, visit the <a href="https://pyrefly.org/">Pyrefly website</a> and the <a href="https://github.com/facebook/pyrefly">Pyrefly GitHub repository</a>.</p>

<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhEXQgyAEhULOnOFhWFIYXZW39BrvFMbqPdg3pFztuFLBgWZux_WlfcY1AlwLu1F9ZU2KwlxF0owAXEpL4rU3SK4oTMfzNguNn6KqhDAh0974imNQ4t1_6wPREMs-k1c3Xgjl9v6huAiNaDh9U_oZr9HZVOw3i35ADbf0tWGZsH-jlRw3wA3twdnGW4OxE/s1600/one-standard.png">
<img class="metadata" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhEXQgyAEhULOnOFhWFIYXZW39BrvFMbqPdg3pFztuFLBgWZux_WlfcY1AlwLu1F9ZU2KwlxF0owAXEpL4rU3SK4oTMfzNguNn6KqhDAh0974imNQ4t1_6wPREMs-k1c3Xgjl9v6huAiNaDh9U_oZr9HZVOw3i35ADbf0tWGZsH-jlRw3wA3twdnGW4OxE/s1600/one-standard.png">

<p>The Apache Iceberg community recently merged a <a href="https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13879">change</a> to the REST Catalog specification that gives lakehouses something they have long been missing: a standard, engine-neutral way to express column masking and row filtering. It is a small change, but it addresses a structural gap in how open table formats handle data governance. This post walks through the problem, the design, and why the details matter.</p>

<figure class="wide borderless">
  <a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhEXQgyAEhULOnOFhWFIYXZW39BrvFMbqPdg3pFztuFLBgWZux_WlfcY1AlwLu1F9ZU2KwlxF0owAXEpL4rU3SK4oTMfzNguNn6KqhDAh0974imNQ4t1_6wPREMs-k1c3Xgjl9v6huAiNaDh9U_oZr9HZVOw3i35ADbf0tWGZsH-jlRw3wA3twdnGW4OxE/s1600/one-standard.png"><img alt="Finally a single fine-grained access control standard for any engine" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhEXQgyAEhULOnOFhWFIYXZW39BrvFMbqPdg3pFztuFLBgWZux_WlfcY1AlwLu1F9ZU2KwlxF0owAXEpL4rU3SK4oTMfzNguNn6KqhDAh0974imNQ4t1_6wPREMs-k1c3Xgjl9v6huAiNaDh9U_oZr9HZVOw3i35ADbf0tWGZsH-jlRw3wA3twdnGW4OxE/s1600/one-standard.png" /></a>
</figure>

<h2>The problem: there is no server in the read path</h2>

<p>In a traditional database, access control is straightforward because there is exactly one door. Every query passes through the database server, the server knows who is asking, and if policy says "this user only sees the last four digits of the card number," the server applies that policy before returning results. One process, one enforcement point.</p>

<p>Apache Iceberg deliberately removed that door. The data is Parquet files in object storage, and any engine—such as BigQuery, Spark, Trino, Flink, PyIceberg, or DuckDB—can read those files directly. This design is what makes Iceberg fast and interoperable. But it also means that once an engine asks the catalog <em>"where is the <code class="inline">payments</code> table?"</em> and receives the metadata pointer, it has full access to the files. The catalog can grant or deny access to the whole table, but it has had no vocabulary for <em>"access granted, but mask the email column"</em> or <em>"access granted, but only on rows where <code class="inline">region = 'US'</code>."</em></p>

<p>Until now, Iceberg had no built-in answer to this. The REST spec did offer coarser instruments like credential vending, which controls storage access per table, and server-side scan planning, which lets a catalog withhold entire data files. But neither can express <em>"mask this column"</em> or filter rows that are not already physically separated into their own files. So users who needed fine-grained access control had to step outside the open protocol entirely. They could adopt a vendor-provided client that understands its proprietary policy format, or route every read through a vendor's proxy service, giving up the direct-to-storage performance that motivated the use of Iceberg in the first place. It also quietly undermines Iceberg's core promise: the moment governance requires a specific vendor's client, the table is no longer open to any engine.</p>

<p>The new <code class="inline">read-restrictions</code> field in the REST Catalog spec is the community standardizing that vocabulary.</p>

<h2>The mechanism</h2>

<p>When an engine calls <code class="inline">loadTable</code>, the response may now include an optional <code class="inline">read-restrictions</code> object:</p>

<figure class="wide borderless">
  <a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiKdDrAf5R0h_5OPiUPLfcQICiwTrXGAqJ_wBSmkaUtEXpv1SlfXhtcf9rTNh1SMVIs7Ag9f9Jtdv7ocKI1AJOu7D7ap1niCZbytzdtcof7o3gyQOixu3Qxg3SnCuiBOt632_3cqkTvCpqd1jrYKDVbJpw3qZuwjtlvH7IUah7gLIsB3Fvii3NsNivEzUI/s1600/payload.png"><img alt="Read restrictions payload showing required column projections and required row projections" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiKdDrAf5R0h_5OPiUPLfcQICiwTrXGAqJ_wBSmkaUtEXpv1SlfXhtcf9rTNh1SMVIs7Ag9f9Jtdv7ocKI1AJOu7D7ap1niCZbytzdtcof7o3gyQOixu3Qxg3SnCuiBOt632_3cqkTvCpqd1jrYKDVbJpw3qZuwjtlvH7IUah7gLIsB3Fvii3NsNivEzUI/s1600/payload.png" /></a>
</figure>

<p>Read restrictions are expressed in two fields:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong><code class="inline">required-row-filter</code></strong>: a standard Iceberg predicate expression. Rows for which it evaluates to false must not appear in the result, and no information derived from them may be included.</li>
  <li><strong><code class="inline">required-column-projections</code></strong>: a list of columns, identified by field ID, each with a transformation the reader must apply before returning values.</li>
</ul>

<p>One evaluation rule ties them together: <strong>the row filter is evaluated against the original, untransformed column values, and projections are applied to the rows that survive.</strong> This ordering is what makes the two features composable. A policy can filter on <code class="inline">region = 'US'</code> and also mask <code class="inline">region</code> in the output, and the filter still works. If masking ran first, any policy that filtered on a masked column would silently break.</p>

<p>Note what the catalog is doing here. It evaluates the access policy server-side—it knows the caller's identity from the authentication token—and returns only the <em>result</em> of that evaluation. The policy itself, with its roles, tags, and governance model, never crosses the wire. The engine does not need to understand how any particular catalog models governance. It needs to understand nine actions and a predicate.</p>

<p>The whole architecture fits in one sequence:</p>

<figure class="wide borderless">
  <a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi0wMil9FpdXzE62JjByQlxedOTfGYhwv5KsZWdGGms_TQgTfQRH4Ex_RkW4OIl_f3CDTyv2o3m3QWH6izLHQo4JiTOu5KwX18WLChGPC8BotkicmU1XE759f_0YpJSaIzotsh67NavzTwIRzOojzq46bWRB2ZBoFrgleaMd6gJJ4yhdqaajd8Tla_bURc/s1600/read-restrictions.png"><img alt="Sequence diagram illustrating the Lakehouse credential vending and reader-side fine-grained access control workflow between an End User, a Trusted Engine (BigQuery/Spark), the Lakehouse runtime catalog, and Google Cloud Storage (GCS)." src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi0wMil9FpdXzE62JjByQlxedOTfGYhwv5KsZWdGGms_TQgTfQRH4Ex_RkW4OIl_f3CDTyv2o3m3QWH6izLHQo4JiTOu5KwX18WLChGPC8BotkicmU1XE759f_0YpJSaIzotsh67NavzTwIRzOojzq46bWRB2ZBoFrgleaMd6gJJ4yhdqaajd8Tla_bURc/s1600/read-restrictions.png" /></a>
  <figcaption><em>The catalog stays the policy decision point; the trusted engine becomes the policy enforcement point; the end user never holds storage credentials. Sections below unpack the three load-bearing details in this picture: the enforcement ordering, the fail-closed branch, and the trust boundary.</em></figcaption>
</figure>

<h2>The nine masking actions</h2>

<p>The specification defines a closed set of nine masking actions, each with an exact, per-type definition. The goal is cross-engine consistency: Spark, Trino, and PyIceberg must produce <em>identical</em> output for any given masking action. These actions are being implemented in <code class="inline">iceberg-core</code>, providing engines with spec-compliant transformations out of the box rather than requiring them to reimplement byte-level logic independently.</p>

<p>Below, the actions are grouped by the analytical utility of the resulting masked data:</p>

<p><strong>Preserve the shape, hide the value</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><code class="inline">mask-alphanum</code>—digits become <code class="inline">n</code>, other characters become <code class="inline">x</code>, with a small allowlist of punctuation (<code class="inline">( ) , . - @</code>) preserved. <code class="inline">iceberg16112018@apache.org</code> becomes <code class="inline">xxxxxxxnnnnnnnn@xxxxxx.xxx</code>—recognizably an email address, but not whose.</li>
  <li><code class="inline">show-first-4</code> / <code class="inline">show-last-4</code>—preserve four code points, and apply <code class="inline">mask-alphanum</code> to the rest. <code class="inline">4111-1111-1111-4444</code> becomes <code class="inline">nnnn-nnnn-nnnn-4444</code>, the familiar customer-support view of a card number.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Hide everything</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><code class="inline">replace-with-null</code>—the value becomes NULL. Only valid for optional fields; a server must not return it for a required field, and a reader that receives one must fail the query.</li>
  <li><code class="inline">mask-to-fixed-value</code>—the value becomes a type-specific constant (<code class="inline">0</code>, <code class="inline">"XXXXXXXX"</code>, the epoch, an all-zero UUID, an empty list, and so on, each spelled out in the spec). Uniquely among the actions, this one also replaces NULL inputs—even the null-or-not bit is hidden.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Reduce precision</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><code class="inline">truncate-to-year</code> / <code class="inline">truncate-to-month</code>—<code class="inline">2024-07-15</code> becomes <code class="inline">2024-01-01</code> or <code class="inline">2024-07-01</code>. Cohort analytics keeps working; identifying individuals gets harder.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Allow joins, hide values</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><code class="inline">sha-256-global</code>—deterministic SHA-256, with exact byte-encoding rules per input type. The same input always produces the same output, everywhere, so <code class="inline">GROUP BY user_id</code> and joins across tables on a hashed key still work. The cost of that determinism is that hashed values can be tested against precomputed guesses—this is pseudonymization, not encryption.</li>
  <li><code class="inline">sha-256-query-local</code>—the same hash, salted with a fresh, cryptographically random salt (at least 16 bytes) per query. Values remain consistent within a single query, so self-joins and aggregation work, but cannot be correlated across queries, and precomputed-guess attacks no longer apply.</li>
</ul>

<p>This last pair is a nice piece of design: the tradeoff between linkability and privacy, expressed as two enum values that a policy author chooses between per column.</p>

<p>Every action produces a value of the same type as its input—masked strings are strings, truncated dates are dates—so restrictions never change the schema an engine plans against. Queries do not need rewriting; values simply arrive transformed.</p>

<h2>Fail-closed by design</h2>

<p>The most consequential sentence in the specification is this one:</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>If a trusted reader that supports read-restrictions cannot apply any returned restriction, it must fail the query and must not silently return raw, partial, or empty results.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Consider the failure modes. A catalog sends an action added in a future spec version that the engine does not recognize. Or an expression type it cannot evaluate. The convenient behavior would be to skip what it does not understand and return the data. The spec rules this out: unrecognized action, fail; unparseable filter, fail; duplicate field ID in the projections, fail. Every ambiguity resolves to "no data" rather than "raw data." This is the right default for an access control mechanism, and it is also the one implementers would be tempted to soften—which is exactly why it is normative in the spec rather than left to judgment. It is also what allows the action vocabulary to grow in future versions without older engines becoming silent leak vectors.</p>

<p>A few prohibitions in the spec reward a closer look, because each one closes a subtle correctness hole:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>No projections on map keys.</strong> Masking a map's keys can collapse two keys into one, or produce null keys, which engines silently coalesce or reject—data corruption presented as privacy. The spec bans it outright.</li>
  <li><strong>No projection on both a nested type and a field inside it.</strong> Masking a struct and also a field within that struct has no well-defined order of operations, so the spec refuses to define one: servers must not send it, and readers must reject it.</li>
  <li><strong>Everything references field IDs, never column names.</strong> This is standard Iceberg discipline: if <code class="inline">ssn</code> is renamed to <code class="inline">national_id</code>, the policy remains bound to the same physical column. A name-based policy would silently detach on rename—the worst possible failure mode for access control.</li>
</ul>

<h2>The trust model, stated plainly</h2>

<p>All of this is enforced by the reader. The catalog hands the engine the file locations along with the restrictions, and a client that chooses to ignore the restrictions can read the raw files. So what is this actually protecting?</p>

<p>The specification is explicit: this mechanism assumes a trust relationship between the catalog and the engine, and how that trust is established is deliberately out of scope. The intended deployment is one where a platform team's engines—the shared Spark and Trino clusters—are trusted enforcement points that hold storage access (for example, through credential vending), while end users only ever talk to those engines and never hold storage credentials themselves. The trusted engine becomes the enforcement point, playing the role the database server played in the traditional architecture. The difference is that its behavior is now defined by a common, open protocol rather than by N proprietary integrations.</p>

<p>In other words, read restrictions do not protect data <em>from</em> the engine; they let the catalog direct a trusted engine to protect data from the engine's users. For genuinely untrusted readers, the coarse-grained model still applies: they are restricted to vended credentials where the storage access granted to the user aligns with the data permission of the user.</p>

<p>One operational subtlety deserves attention: restrictions are per-response and per-identity. The same <code class="inline">loadTable</code> call made by a different principal—or by the same principal later—may return different restrictions, and the restrictions attach to every read performed with that response, including subsequent <code class="inline">planTableScan</code> and <code class="inline">fetchScanTasks</code> calls. The spec therefore requires that the response not be cached outside its authentication scope. If your platform caches <code class="inline">loadTableResponse</code>, that cache is now security-sensitive and worth an audit.</p>

<h2>What is still missing</h2>

<p>Read restrictions are a foundation, not the finished building. It is worth being honest about the gaps between this specification and complete fine-grained access control:</p>

<ol>
  <li><strong>The action vocabulary is fixed, because Iceberg Expressions are not implemented yet.</strong> Nine actions cover the common masking policies, but they are a deliberately closed set: a policy like "apply this custom redaction function" cannot be expressed, and the row filter is limited to predicates—comparisons that produce true or false. The path to generalizing this already exists on paper: the <a href="https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/587f7984ff811b1240b0ccf8e34e73e1a52f94d0/format/expressions-spec.md">Iceberg Expressions specification</a>, proposed by Ryan Blue and adopted in mid-2026, defines a portable structure for value expressions—constants, field references, and calls to well-defined functions or <a href="https://iceberg.apache.org/udf-spec/">SQL UDFs</a>. Once engines can evaluate those expressions, a catalog could return arbitrary transformations instead of choosing from an enum. Today no engine implements general expression evaluation, which is why the initial design confines itself to a small vocabulary that can be specified bit-for-bit.</li>
  <li><strong>There is no policy definition—deliberately.</strong> The specification standardizes the <em>result</em> of policy evaluation, never the policy itself. How an organization expresses "analysts see masked PII, auditors see everything"—the roles, tags, rules, and administrative APIs—remains entirely the catalog vendor's domain, and the assumption is that it stays there. Only the consequences of a policy are portable across engines; the policy definition is not. Whether communities eventually want a portable policy format is an open question the spec does not attempt to answer.</li>
  <li><strong>Trusted clients are asserted, not proven.</strong> As the trust-model section noted, how a catalog establishes that a caller is a trusted, enforcing engine is out of scope. In practice that trust is deployment configuration—service identities, network boundaries, and which principals receive vended credentials. There is no attestation mechanism in the protocol by which an engine proves it enforces restrictions; the trusted-client mechanism is an assumption the platform operator must make true.</li>
</ol>

<p>None of these gaps undermines the design—each is a deliberate scoping decision that kept the proposal small enough to reach consensus—but they define the roadmap for what "complete" fine-grained access control in the open lakehouse still requires.</p>

<h2>Why this matters</h2>

<p>The specification change itself does not ship enforcement; that work in the engines begins now, starting with the default actions. But the shape of the design is right in three ways:</p>

<ol>
  <li><strong>It picks the honest enforcement point.</strong> In an architecture with no server in the read path, the trusted engine is the only place enforcement can live without giving up direct storage reads. The spec accepts that constraint explicitly rather than obscuring it.</li>
  <li><strong>It standardizes the narrow waist.</strong> Catalogs keep their own rich policy engines—roles, tags, and attribute-based rules. Engines implement nine actions and a predicate evaluator, once. N×M becomes N+M.</li>
  <li><strong>It is fail-closed everywhere</strong>, which is what makes the vocabulary safely extensible.</li>
</ol>

<p>The pattern—the catalog evaluates policy against the caller's identity and returns a small, closed vocabulary of obligations that the client must enforce or fail—is a useful template, and it would not be surprising to see more of the governance surface expressed this way over time.</p>

<p>The proposal was approved on the Apache Iceberg dev list with eight binding +1 votes and no objections. This is a strong signal of consensus across the many companies and open source communities that participate in the project. Consistent, engine-independent enforcement of fine-grained policies is a property the ecosystem has long wanted; it now has a specification for it, and the interesting work of implementing it in engines and catalogs is underway. If you work on either, the <a href="https://lists.apache.org/list.html?dev@iceberg.apache.org">dev list</a> is the place to get involved.</p>

View the full <a href="https://lists.apache.org/thread/0zloqhp8wkgyn04yg69j71cwcg5n7g74">vote thread</a>.</em></p>

<p>Did you know the Google Chrome Wikipedia page received over 36 million page views in 2025, or that Chromium logged over 3,700 commits in April 2010? If you have needed large, real-world datasets to benchmark query engines on Apache Iceberg, Google Cloud’s Lakehouse team is excited to announce the release of new public datasets in Google Cloud Lakehouse to help you explore and analyze open data at scale.</p>

<p>Google Cloud’s Lakehouse provides a high-performance storage catalog using Apache Iceberg as its open table format. By decoupling storage from compute, it enables you to use your preferred query engines—such as BigQuery, Apache Spark, or Trino—while managing data in an open format to avoid vendor lock-in.</p>

<p>These new public datasets are designed to help you explore the Apache Iceberg ecosystem and begin working immediately with real-world data. We are providing access to some of the most popular BigQuery public datasets, including Wikipedia pageviews and GitHub commit histories. Let’s dive into how you can start querying them.</p>

<h2>Prerequisites</h2>
<ul>
  <li>A Google Cloud project (for authentication).</li>
  <li>Standard Google Application Default Credentials (ADC) configured in your environment.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Explore metadata with PyIceberg</h2>
<p>To explore table metadata using PyIceberg, install the required Python packages in a virtual environment:</p>

<pre><code class="codebox bash">sudo apt-get install python3-venv
python3 -m venv public_data_lakehouse
source public_data_lakehouse/bin/activate
pip install google-auth
pip install pyiceberg
pip install pyarrow</code></pre>

<p>After installing the required packages, you can inspect a table’s schema using the Python script below. Here is how to inspect the table containing Wikipedia page view data from 2016:</p>

<pre><code class="codebox python">from pyiceberg import catalog as pyiceberg_catalog

PROJECT = "&lt;YOUR_PROJECT_ID&gt;"
NAMESPACE = "wikipedia"
TABLE = "pageviews_2016"

def load_catalog() -&gt; pyiceberg_catalog.Catalog:
  properties = {
      "type": "rest",
      "uri": "https://biglake.googleapis.com/iceberg/v1/restcatalog",
      "warehouse": "gs://lakehouse-public-data",
      "auth": {"type": "google"},
      "header.X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation": "vended-credentials",
      "header.x-goog-user-project": PROJECT,
  }
  return pyiceberg_catalog.load_catalog(PROJECT, **properties)

def main() -&gt; None:
  catalog = load_catalog()
  table = catalog.load_table((NAMESPACE, TABLE))
  print(f"Schema for `{NAMESPACE}.{TABLE}`:", table.schema())

if __name__ == "__main__":
  main()</code></pre>

<p><em>Note: Replace <code class="inline python">&lt;YOUR_PROJECT_ID&gt;</code> with your actual Google Cloud Project ID. This is required for the REST catalog to authenticate your quota usage, even for free public access.</em></p>

<h2>PySpark and Managed Service for Apache Spark</h2>
<p>Now that we have explored the table’s schema, we can use a managed, serverless Spark notebook to query the tables. This provides the speed and flexibility of Apache Spark without creating or managing a cluster. You can run this script in Google Cloud's serverless Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Dataproc):</p>

<pre><code class="codebox python">from google.cloud.dataproc_v1 import Session
from google.cloud.dataproc_spark_connect import DataprocSparkSession

PROJECT_ID = "&lt;YOUR_PROJECT_ID&gt;"
spark_catalog = "lakehouse-public-data"

session = Session()
session.runtime_config.properties = {
  "spark.sql.extensions": "org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions.IcebergSparkSessionExtensions",
  f"spark.sql.catalog.{spark_catalog}": "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog",
  f"spark.sql.catalog.{spark_catalog}.type": "rest",
  f"spark.sql.catalog.{spark_catalog}.uri": "https://biglake.googleapis.com/iceberg/v1/restcatalog",
  f"spark.sql.catalog.{spark_catalog}.rest.auth.type": "org.apache.iceberg.gcp.auth.GoogleAuthManager",
  f"spark.sql.catalog.{spark_catalog}.io-impl": "org.apache.iceberg.gcp.gcs.GCSFileIO",
  f"spark.sql.catalog.{spark_catalog}.header.X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation": "vended-credentials",
  f"spark.sql.catalog.{spark_catalog}.warehouse": "gs://lakehouse-public-data",
  f"spark.sql.catalog.{spark_catalog}.header.x-goog-user-project": PROJECT_ID,
}

spark = (
   DataprocSparkSession.builder
     .appName("Lakehouse Public Data Demo")
     .dataprocSessionConfig(session)
     .getOrCreate()
)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.defaultCatalog", spark_catalog)</code></pre>

<p>With the session active, you can query monthly Wikipedia view counts for BigQuery-related articles by executing the following code in a new cell:</p>

<pre><code class="codebox python">df1 = spark.sql("""
SELECT
  title,
  wiki,
  SUM(views) AS total_views
FROM wikipedia.pageviews_2026
WHERE datehour &gt;= TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00'
  AND datehour &lt;  TIMESTAMP '2026-02-01 00:00:00'
  AND LOWER(title) LIKE '%bigquery%'
GROUP BY title, wiki
ORDER BY total_views DESC
LIMIT 20
""")
df1.show(10)</code></pre>

<p>Or, you can retrieve recent GitHub commits referencing Iceberg using the following snippet:</p>

<pre><code class="codebox python">df2 = spark.sql("""
SELECT
  commits.commit,
  commits.subject,
  commits.message,
  commits.author.name AS author_name,
  timestamp_seconds(commits.committer.date.seconds) AS commit_time,
  repo_name
FROM github_repos.commits AS commits
WHERE LOWER(commits.subject) LIKE '%iceberg%'
   OR LOWER(commits.message) LIKE '%iceberg%'
ORDER BY commit_time DESC
LIMIT 50
""")
df2.show(10)</code></pre>

<h2>Start building today</h2>
<p>These datasets were imported from their BigQuery counterparts and transformed using Apache Iceberg as the table format and Parquet as the data file format. Our goal is to lower the entry barrier so you can learn and explore Apache Iceberg with your favorite query engine without managing any infrastructure. To get started with building an open, managed, and high-performance Iceberg lakehouse, visit the <a href="https://cloud.google.com/products/lakehouse">Google Cloud Lakehouse page</a>.</p>

<h2>This Week in Open Source for September 24, 2026</h2>
<p><em>A look around the world of open source</em></p>

<p>Open source underpins an $8.8 trillion global economy, yet sustaining it requires moving beyond voluntary charity and philosophical appeals. This week’s reads examine how the ecosystem is adapting to modern economic and AI pressures—from proposing package-registry royalties and quantifying 2–5x net value for regulated utility grids, to turning autonomous AI security incidents into hardened supply-chain defenses that empower open-science breakthroughs like NASA and IBM’s Lunar Foundation Model.</p>

<h2>Upcoming Events</h2>

Dedicated Linux Foundation developer summit advancing the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and open agentic interoperability standards. Join Google OSPO's Daryl Ducharme on October 6 for <em>"Tag-Team Transmission: Navigating A2A and MCP for Optimum Orchestration,"</em> examining how the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol and MCP interoperate across multi-agent architectures.</li>

<h2>Open Source Reads and Links</h2>
<ul>
<li>[Blog] <a href="https://seldo.com/posts/nobody-pays-for-open-source-we-can-force-them-to/">Nobody pays for open source. We can force them to.</a> — Companies already spend over $1 billion a year on open source, but that money goes to supply-chain mirror and security vendors rather than the maintainers writing the code. Laurie Voss breaks down why voluntary charity and license changes always fail, arguing that commercial package registries and mirror vendors should pay automatic royalties down the dependency tree to long-tail maintainers.</li>
<li>[Article] <a href="https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1144074">AI Is reshaping open source software and straining the systems that sustain it</a> — As conversations grow around moderating the speed of AI development across the industry, it is critical to watch the friction points where AI and open source overlap—particularly as an influx of AI-generated code and vulnerability discovery strains maintainers of an $8.8 trillion ecosystem. Funding remains front and center, requiring not just raw capital but continuous monitoring for effectiveness in sustaining the human governance, consensus-building, and non-coding infrastructure that AI cannot replace.</li>
<li>[Report] <a href="https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/lf-energy-research-finds-open-source-software-can-deliver-2-5x-greater-net-value-for-grid-operators">LF Energy Research Finds Open Source Software Can Deliver 2-5x Greater Net Value for Grid Operators</a> — While open source software and public utilities seem like natural philosophical allies as public goods, philosophical appeals routinely fail in regulated infrastructure sectors where operators are bound by strict reliability mandates and ratepayer accountability. This new LF Energy report demonstrates how to bridge that gap: by translating collaborative "make together" governance into an auditable benefit-cost framework showing two to five times greater net value over proprietary procurement.</li>
<li>[Article] <a href="https://time.com/article/2026/09/09/ai-is-at-a-turning-point/">AI Is at a Turning Point</a> — High-profile incidents of autonomous AI agents breaching Hugging Face or social-engineering open source maintainers inevitably dominate headlines and amplify purely negative narratives around AI. However, treating these security failures as concrete post-mortems—exposing how standard reinforcement learning incentivizes deceptive subgoals—is exactly what allows open source communities to establish hardened supply-chain defenses and safely advance high-impact, positive AI use cases.</li>
<li>[Article] <a href="https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-09-10-ibm-and-nasa-release-open-source-ai-model-to-support-lunar-exploration">IBM and NASA Release Open-Source AI Model to Support Lunar Exploration</a> — Seeing open source, AI, open data, and space science converge is genuinely inspiring, especially when it demonstrates that open scientific models are only as useful as the open datasets beneath them. While NASA and JAXA planetary archives have long been public, IBM and NASA's release of the Lunar Foundation Model alongside the first harmonized, machine-learning-ready lunar dataset (unifying 30+ multi-instrument layers) proves that transforming raw open data into shared, interoperable infrastructure is what unlocks domain discovery.</li>
</ul>

<p>Google Cloud is committed to open source, and PostgreSQL is a cornerstone of managed database offerings, including Cloud SQL and AlloyDB.</p>

<p>Continuing our work with the PostgreSQL communities, we've been contributing to the core engine and participating in the patch review process. Below is a summary of that technical activity between January 2026 and September 2026, highlighting our efforts to enhance the performance, stability, and resilience of the upstream project and ecosystem. By strengthening these core capabilities, we aim to drive innovation that benefits the entire global PostgreSQL ecosystem and its diverse user base.</p>

<p>Our technical contributions in this period have focused on enhancing core engine performance, introducing features for logical replication, fixing critical bugs, and improving upgrade resilience. We also continue to invest in the PostgreSQL ecosystem by addressing bugs in widely used extensions.</p>

<h2>Technical contributions: January 2026 – September 2026</h2>

<p>Our contributions this cycle span four key areas:</p>

<ol>
  <li><strong>Logical replication and conflict management</strong>: Paving the way for active-active replication, enhanced conflict logging, and catalog safety.</li>
  <li><strong>Core engine performance and reliability</strong>: Eliminating tuple-level overhead in sequential scans and making promotion timeouts accurate.</li>
  <li><strong>Core catalog, collation, and indexing bug fixes</strong>: Strengthening privilege consistency, deferrable index builds, collation handling, and memory safety.</li>
  <li><strong>PostgreSQL extension and ecosystem hardening</strong>: Resolving critical crashes, lock tranche registrations, and memory vulnerabilities across popular ecosystem extensions (<code class="inline">plpgsql_check</code>, <code class="inline">pgfincore</code>, and <code class="inline">pgtt</code>).</li>
</ol>

<h3>1. Logical replication and conflict management</h3>

<p>Logical replication is essential for near-zero downtime migrations, major version upgrades, and multi-region data distribution. Our recent work focuses on conflict log table infrastructure, namespace clarity, and cross-database catalog hygiene.</p>

<h4><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/E1wf7cJ-0011jL-2F%40gemulon.postgresql.org#:~:text=Author%3A%20Dilip%20Kumar%20%3Cdilipbalaut(at)gmail(dot)com%3E">Conflict log table infrastructure</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Background and challenge</strong>: A major milestone on the roadmap to active-active multi-master replication is the ability to automatically record and resolve data discrepancies across nodes. Without structured conflict logs, tracking conflicting writes requires inspecting server logs or relying on custom application handlers.</li>
  <li><strong>Solution</strong>: This patch introduces the foundational conflict log table management infrastructure as an option in <code class="inline">CREATE SUBSCRIPTION</code>. It establishes the catalog structures and configuration hooks necessary to direct conflict records into dedicated, queryable tables, serving as the cornerstone for upcoming automatic conflict logging into tables.</li>
  <li><strong>Note</strong>: Provided no blocking issues arise, this functionality is slated for inclusion in PG 20.</li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Dilip Kumar (Primary Author)</li>
</ul>

<h4><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/E1wl7tC-000nNc-1k%40gemulon.postgresql.org">Fix REASSIGN OWNED for subscriptions in other databases</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Background and challenge</strong>: While <code class="inline">pg_subscription</code> is physically a shared catalog so the background launcher process can scan all databases, subscription objects are logically local to each database. Certain operations, such as <code class="inline">REASSIGN OWNED</code>, failed to restrict their catalog scans to the current database (<code class="inline">MyDatabaseId</code>), leading to accidental modifications across database boundaries.</li>
  <li><strong>Solution</strong>: Added explicit guards to <code class="inline">pg_subscription</code> readers to ensure non-launcher processes filter strictly by <code class="inline">MyDatabaseId</code>, protecting cross-database isolation and updating documentation.</li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Dilip Kumar (Author)</li>
</ul>

<h4><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/E1wLCwb-000oB5-1A%40gemulon.postgresql.org">Schema-qualified names in EXCEPT clause error messages</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Background and challenge</strong>: When publishing tables with <code class="inline">EXCEPT</code> clauses, <code class="inline">check_publication_add_relation()</code> previously reported only unqualified table names when a relation could not be processed, leading to ambiguous error messages in multi-schema databases.</li>
  <li><strong>Solution</strong>: Updated error reporting paths to emit fully schema-qualified relation names, aligning with PostgreSQL's broader error messaging standards.</li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Dilip Kumar (Author)</li>
</ul>

<h3>2. Core engine performance and administrative enhancements</h3>

<p>Optimizing throughput and improving the predictability of administrative operations remain top priorities for database workloads.</p>

<h4><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/E1w5Zie-001T6v-2k%40gemulon.postgresql.org">Timeout handling in pg_promote()</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Background and challenge</strong>: Standby promotion via <code class="inline">pg_promote()</code> allows users to specify a timeout interval. Due to imprecise elapsed-time tracking during wait loops, promotion operations could terminate prematurely before the configured timeout elapsed.</li>
  <li><strong>Solution</strong>: Refined the promotion loop to pre-calculate the expected end timestamp and track actual elapsed time across iterations, ensuring strict adherence to user-configured wait intervals.</li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Robert Pang (Reporter and Author)</li>
</ul>

<h4><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/E1vlbnK-0003nf-2n%40gemulon.postgresql.org">Sequential scan performance optimization</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Background and challenge</strong>: Previously, <code class="inline">CheckXidAlive</code> validation was executed inside the inner <code class="inline">table_scan_next</code> routines. This incurred repetitive check overhead on every single tuple fetched during sequential scans.</li>
  <li><strong>Solution</strong>: Restructured the scan control flow to eliminate redundant per-tuple checks, yielding cleaner execution paths and measurable throughput improvements on large table scans.</li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Dilip Kumar (Author)</li>
</ul>

<h3>3. Core engine access control, collation, and indexing bug fixes</h3>

<p>We continue to harden PostgreSQL's core engine against catalog inconsistencies, segmentation faults, and edge-case query anomalies.</p>

<h4><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/E1vuczI-000sUq-2Z%40gemulon.postgresql.org">Large object access with pg_{read,write}_all_data</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Problem</strong>: The default roles <code class="inline">pg_read_all_data</code> and <code class="inline">pg_write_all_data</code> were designed to allow maintenance utilities like <code class="inline">pg_dump</code> to operate without superuser privileges. However, Large Objects (LOBs) remained inaccessible under these roles without explicit object-level grants.</li>
  <li><strong>Fix</strong>: Updated permission checks to extend <code class="inline">pg_read_all_data</code> and <code class="inline">pg_write_all_data</code> coverage to Large Objects, completing superuser-free dump and maintenance workflows.</li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Nitin Motiani (Author), Dilip Kumar (Reviewer)</li>
</ul>

<h4><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/E1woV96-00000000a2q-0X8s%40gemulon.postgresql.org">Immediate property propagation in index copies (REINDEX CONCURRENTLY)</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Problem</strong>: When building a replacement index during <code class="inline">REINDEX CONCURRENTLY</code> for a deferrable unique constraint, <code class="inline">index_create_copy()</code> defaulted constraint flags to 0, setting the immediate property to true. This caused concurrent transactions to immediately trigger constraint violations rather than deferring verification until commit time.</li>
  <li><strong>Fix</strong>: Introduced the <code class="inline">INDEX_CREATE_DEFERRABLE</code> flag to properly propagate an immediate property of false to transient copied indexes without violating internal constraint assertions.</li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Nitin Motiani (Author)</li>
</ul>

<h4><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/E1wgoMZ-001d4O-1K%40gemulon.postgresql.org">LIKE matching with nondeterministic collations and backslashes</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Problem</strong>: Following the addition of nondeterministic collation support for <code class="inline">LIKE</code>, literal pattern substring parsing unconditionally skipped all backslash characters. When encountering escaped backslashes (<code class="inline">\\</code>), the engine omitted the second backslash entirely instead of emitting a literal <code class="inline">\</code>.</li>
  <li><strong>Fix</strong>: Corrected pattern de-escaping logic to correctly recognize and emit escaped backslashes during evaluation.</li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Nitin Motiani (Author)</li>
</ul>

<h4><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/E1vgbPL-000jxT-2O%40gemulon.postgresql.org">DSM lock release and crash prevention</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Problem</strong>: If a backend encountered a <code class="inline">FATAL</code> exit while holding a lock in a Dynamic Shared Memory (DSM) segment (e.g., inside dynamic shared hashtables <code class="inline">dshash</code>) outside of an active transaction, releasing locks during process termination could reference already detached DSM segments, triggering a segmentation fault.</li>
  <li><strong>Fix</strong>: Hardened cleanup and lock release sequences during fatal exits to safely detach memory segments without segfaulting.</li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Dilip Kumar (Reviewer)</li>
</ul>

<h3>4. PostgreSQL ecosystem and extension hardening</h3>

<p>Enterprise PostgreSQL architectures rely heavily on third-party extensions. Our team actively contributes bug fixes and stability improvements upstream to critical ecosystem projects.</p>

<h4><a href="https://github.com/okbob/plpgsql_check/pull/215/commits">plpgsql_check: LWLock tranche registration for PG14</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Problem</strong>: In PG14 and earlier, loading <code class="inline">plpgsql_check</code> via <code class="inline">shared_preload_libraries</code> could fail with shared memory lock errors due to missing or outdated named LWLock tranche registrations (<code class="inline">plpgsql_check profiler funcs stats</code> and <code class="inline">plpgsql_check profiler func stmts stats</code>).</li>
  <li><strong>Fix</strong>: Aligned pre-PG15 tranche initialization with modern <code class="inline">shmem_request_hook</code> patterns, guaranteeing safe shared memory allocation on older server versions.</li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Aniket Jha (Author)</li>
</ul>

<h4><a href="https://github.com/klando/pgfincore/pull/12">pgfincore: Memory safety hardening</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Problem</strong>: <code class="inline">pgfincore</code> contained two subtle memory corruption issues: an off-by-one array boundary access during buffer inspection and a dangling pointer assignment during deallocation.</li>
  <li><strong>Fix</strong>: Authored patches to enforce strict boundary checks and clean pointer resets, eliminating potential memory corruption during OS buffer cache analysis.</li>
  <li><strong>PRs</strong>: <a href="https://github.com/klando/pgfincore/pull/12">klando/pgfincore#12</a> and <a href="https://github.com/klando/pgfincore/pull/13">klando/pgfincore#13</a></li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Robert Pang (Author)</li>
</ul>

<h4><a href="https://github.com/darold/pgtt/commit/e949a6c81eeaec6bd0b03c25c7428aa5cb68821f">pgtt: Use-after-free prevention on cached plans</a></h4>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Problem</strong>: When running utility commands via the extended query protocol or within cached contexts (such as PL/pgSQL and SQL functions), <code class="inline">pgtt</code> modified cached statement parse trees in-place using short-lived query memory. Once that memory was freed, subsequent executions of the cached plan led to Use-After-Free crashes.</li>
  <li><strong>Fix</strong>: Updated the extension to operate on an isolated, deep copy of the parse tree for cached and read-only statements, ensuring memory safety across repeated executions.</li>
  <li><strong>Contributors</strong>: Sunaina Punyani (Author)</li>
</ul>

<p>For over twenty years, <a href="https://g.co/gsoc">Google Summer of Code</a> (GSoC) has welcomed new developers into open source by pairing them with experienced mentors on real projects. This spirit is especially vibrant in India, which is home to more than 55% of all global GSoC participants over the last decade.</p>

<p>This July, our team traveled across Bengaluru and Delhi to host a series of developer events and debut our first-ever GSoC Alumni CAMP, bringing together members of India’s vibrant GSoC alumni community. We engaged directly with current and former GSoC Contributors, Mentors, and project maintainers, experiencing firsthand the passion and energy of the Indian developer ecosystem.</p>

<h2>Community stories: Learning to think and lead as an engineer</h2>

<p>In both Bengaluru and Delhi, a highlight of the trip was hearing directly how open source and GSoC have fundamentally changed how developers think and work.</p>

<p>For many attendees, having a dedicated open source mentor through GSoC took the fear out of tackling new and intimidating codebases. One former participant told us they almost walked away from a distributed storage project because it felt too overwhelming: <em>"Storage systems felt impossible. But great mentors taught me how to think, not just how to code."</em> Another echoed that shift in perspective: <em>"Why am I spending so much time thinking rather than coding? Then I realized that building products is actually about thinking more than coding. GSoC taught me to think like an engineer."</em></p>

<p>That shift in mindset turns first-time contributors into long-term open source community leaders. We met one developer who submitted their very first pull request in 2023, started mentoring in 2024, and is now a lead maintainer for <a href="https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=fr.free.nrw.commons&amp;hl=en_US">a major open source Android app</a>. We also saw how new contributors to global projects can spark entire local ecosystems—like the <a href="https://www.meetup.com/bangalore-compilers-meetup-group/">Indian compiler community</a>, which started with a few GSoC alumni and has rapidly grown into a 3,500+ member network with dozens of meetups across the country.</p>

  <a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgUGker7QNLW1ck1VJ99-0QfXXnvsVKHl5HdY9aR51FcHY5HvfXUkYTei-odrap3TuvOgu7YAY08-5kBjWPe_Ha8G0c0raldcAjW5fnnFiJRuvWorfAcoojbHQqgPrDAt_lnkIFMq38Ysfu1FGTPwOPPdjERF1tK_yKtXppcHQocUFEeTpY2y9IUjFiLNY/s1600/gsoc_bengaluru.png"><img alt="Group photo of over a hundred Google Summer of Code alumni, mentors, and organizers wearing blue GSoC t-shirts gathered in front of a stage banner reading Google Summer of Code Alumni CAMP India 2026 in Bengaluru" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgUGker7QNLW1ck1VJ99-0QfXXnvsVKHl5HdY9aR51FcHY5HvfXUkYTei-odrap3TuvOgu7YAY08-5kBjWPe_Ha8G0c0raldcAjW5fnnFiJRuvWorfAcoojbHQqgPrDAt_lnkIFMq38Ysfu1FGTPwOPPdjERF1tK_yKtXppcHQocUFEeTpY2y9IUjFiLNY/s1600/gsoc_bengaluru.png" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto;" /></a>

<h2>Open source mentorship in the age of AI</h2>

<p>Across our sessions and unconference discussions, one recurring conversation resonated above all others: the evolving role of mentorship in an AI-assisted world. The human element of open source is more critical than ever. As one attendee noted:</p>

<blockquote>
  <p><em>AI can generate the slides, but the context takes nine years.</em></p>
</blockquote>

<p>We heard over and over from participants—open source maintainer time and attention remains a limited resource. CAMP participants presented multiple examples of where AI is proving effective for generating starter templates, writing tests, or fixing syntax. Even with this, what open source projects fundamentally need hasn't changed: maintainer time, clear architectural vision, and thoughtful code reviews.</p>

<p>Beyond code quality, the industry agrees that <a href="https://github.blog/open-source/maintainers/rethinking-open-source-mentorship-in-the-ai-era/">dedicated mentorship is the vital bridge</a> between temporary contributions and long-term project stewardship. Without structured guidance, newcomers often struggle with unwritten project norms, complex codebase histories, or public review feedback, leading to contributor burnout and abandoned pull requests. Programs like GSoC transform casual interest into a sustainable maintainer pipeline by fostering psychological safety, belonging, and accountable relationships. <strong>By investing directly in maintainer time and human connection, GSoC ensures that open source projects remain secure and resilient for generations to come.</strong></p>

<h2>What’s next?</h2>

<p>If our trip across Bengaluru and Delhi taught us anything, it’s that the strength of open source has always come from the communities we build together, not the volume of code any one person can ship.</p>

<p>As developer tools evolve, our main focus for GSoC is preserving the mentorship experience that makes the program special. Manually sifting through low-quality, automated submissions wastes maintainer time and drains the energy of volunteers who signed up to mentor new peers and colleagues. We're ready to tackle these challenges directly by optimizing our program to assist and protect our community of open source maintainers, so <em>they</em> can focus on leading their open source projects and helping new engineers grow. You can stay updated on GSoC’s program rules and timelines at <a href="https://g.co/gsoc">g.co/gsoc</a>.</p>
