While this source provides a historical record of open source development on GitHub, as a real-time or comprehensive source of metrics, it's unreliable and should not be a source for volume-based metrics.&nbsp;</span></p><br /><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">In 2025, GHarchive captured 14% fewer events than in 2024, despite steady growth in </span><a href="https://innovationgraph.github.com/global-metrics/repositories" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">platform adoption</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">.&nbsp; Since 2025, we estimate that data retention in GHarchive has fallen to ~50% and in 2026 it may be as low as 20% for some event types (see figure below). Prior to 2025, you could make the general assumption that the majority of </span><a href="https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/github-event-types" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">events</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> would be represented in this pipeline. Since 2025, we must now assume we may be missing at least half of events and possibly more — not to mention all of the additional activity that’s left out of the event API (see GitHub’s </span><a href="https://docs.github.com/en/graphql" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">GraphQL</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> API.)&nbsp;</span></p><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"><img height="368" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEhWI1EZBXgBioSYJ4vwVDAv5EZxIsFj7tna-3C-FSrZ5d-eCgOQIj97eycf_kjPnZW7JfRZyfYdbf6Wai8yIQEotI8pAbCkaxYREItO_MrZeZoNmweU2n42AXxTx4gZdRTThCuL4V6iyEnVU3hPx1BKn14hzP2Ro3rOHt4FL7ZFCH8zTaq_v1N2wPoSmb-X" style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; border: none;" width="597" /></span></p><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">The </span><a href="https://github.com/igrigorik/gharchive.org" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">crawler</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> logic behind this dataset is simple: give me all the events from the </span><a href="https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/github-event-types" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">GitHub Event</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> stream (e.g. opening pull requests, commenting on issues etc). However, the GitHub API has </span><a href="https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">limitations</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> on the number of calls per hour as well as the number of events listed, so for days with a lot of spiky activity, the crawler will miss some. Although we never assumed that this dataset was collecting 100% of events, the current architecture is showing signs of strain. We suspect that this is due, in part, to the rate of </span><a href="https://innovationgraph.github.com/global-metrics/repositories" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">repository growth</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> and adoption of automated tooling on GitHub. In 2011, GitHub announced it reached </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_GitHub" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">2 million public repositories</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">, and by 2026, that figure surpassed </span><a href="https://innovationgraph.github.com/global-metrics/repositories" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">400 million.</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">&nbsp;&nbsp;</span></p><br /><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">I want to acknowledge that </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; font-weight: 700; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">building and sharing comprehensive open datasets at scale is hard. </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">Have you ever built a pipeline only to discover that the variables changed mid year, the payload for one output is getting truncated, all your joins broke because one side of the dataset is case sensitive … I could go on. And these examples are just ordinary data issues. Building a dataset at the scale of GitHub where “Every second, </span><a href="https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-a-new-developer-joins-github-every-second-as-ai-leads-typescript-to-1/" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">more than one new developer on average joined GitHub—over 36 million in the past year</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">”—you start running into a new set of challenges.</span></p><br /><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">My own journey with open source related data began when I repeatedly found myself questioning how much we could trust our own </span><a href="https://opensource.googleblog.com/2026/08/adapting-open-source-practices-to-an-ai-first-world-a-retrospective-on-2025.html" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">metrics</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">. To expand my understanding of the nuances and the limitations of open source related datasets, I reached out to </span><a href="https://nesbitt.io/" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">Andrew Nesbitt</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">, who has spent years digging in data trenches for the benefit of the community. Together we converged on the following issues that we wanted to highlight for the broader community.</span></p><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span style="font-size: 20pt; white-space: pre-wrap;"><br /></span></p><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span style="font-size: 20pt; white-space: pre-wrap;">Assembling: Assume there will be problems</span></p><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">When I asked Andrew </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-style: italic; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">‘can you summarize the challenges you have faced assembling comprehensive datasets?’ —</span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; font-weight: 700; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">“I just assume I'm going to have a terrible time anyway, so I start with my best effort and fill in the gaps”. </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">While disappointing, this aligned with most data aggregation methods I’ve reviewed—tools such as </span><a href="https://chaoss.github.io/grimoirelab/" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">Grimoire labs</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> and </span><a href="https://ossinsight.io/" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">OSS insights</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> also require multiple processes for collection, combination and reconciliation. Even with these approaches, many sources have missing, incomplete, or inconsistent information.</span></p><br /><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; font-weight: 700; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">One source is probably not enough. </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">If you are considering the use of an open source project, you may want to know how many maintainers work on this project, what versions are available, what their dependencies are and any active vulnerabilities or known issues. Each of these queries requires a distinct source—the development history, the dependency graph, the CVE database, etc. </span><a href="http://ecosyste.ms" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">Ecosyste.ms</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> strives to pull this information together into one place, but combining data from 1000+ datasets has its own unique set of challenges.</span></p><br /><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">For example, </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; font-weight: 700; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">my index is probably not your index. </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">One perennial issue is inconsistent naming conventions across sources. Beyond variable type and format, repository names, versions, packages, tags, licenses, urls, etc. tend to be unique across platforms. Some are case sensitive, there are often duplicates, and anyone can change a name at any time… I’ve been keenly following the adoption of </span><a href="https://github.com/package-url" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">purl</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> and </span><a href="https://www.softwareheritage.org/software-hash-identifier-swhid/" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">SWHID</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">, but so far I have not found one name to rule them all.</span></p><br /><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; font-weight: 700; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">Now we have to keep this up to date: </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">At the moment, there is no consistent way of sharing updates across platforms. Changes to names, APIs, deletions, etc. are more often discovered by errors and breakage than by scouring release notes. To keep Ecosyste.ms up to date, Andrew has written multiple </span><a href="https://github.com/ecosyste-ms/repos/blob/main/docs/syncing.md" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">syncing processes</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> that identify or infer updates that need to be accounted for. I asked Andrew ‘</span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-style: italic; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">If you could ask a platform/data source to change one thing, what would it be?’, </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; font-weight: 700; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">“Can I crawl an endpoint that's just NEW stuff?’</span></p><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span style="font-size: 20pt; white-space: pre-wrap;"><br /></span></p><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span style="font-size: 20pt; white-space: pre-wrap;">Consuming: Design your pipeline for your use case</span></p><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">Because of LLMs,</span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; font-weight: 700; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"> “it's now easier for anyone to try to access and build reports”</span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">. But those building quick reports are likely not going to go through the pain of being comprehensive. This is where aggregated sources like GHarchive and Ecosyste.ms thrive. As data providers, we’d love if data consumers knew that:</span></p><br /><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; font-weight: 700; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">How you collect data matters. </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">If everyone wanted the same dataset, in the same format, at the same time, it would be simple. Depending on how the data is stored—centralized vs distributed and cached, relational vs graph, etc. —queries could be more efficient (in cost and computation) than exports or bulk requests faster than individual requests. This all depends on the topology of the infrastructure and the dataset. In a perfect world, data producers would design their architecture for their top user journeys. However open source related datasets serve a wide variety of user personas from corporations to non-profits, researchers to individual users, maintainers, funders, and many more, with a variety of demands from historical deep dives to realtime feedback. Data producers can’t design for all of these cases, so my challenge to them is to be more open about the best way to access this information.&nbsp;</span></p><br /><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">At the end of the day, we have to </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; font-weight: 700; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">respect the </span><a href="https://www.opensourcestories.org/stories/2023/critical-human-infrastructure/" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; font-weight: 700; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">human infrastructure</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; font-weight: 700; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">: </span><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">Open source-related datasets are riddled with personally identifiable information (PII). Some individuals may be comfortable sharing their information with fellow contributors, but seeing it aggregated across platforms can be uncomfortable. Any source with PII should be handled with care: anonymize when you can and ensure you are in alignment with policies and regulations. Open source communities are real people so please, consume their data responsibly.</span></p><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span style="font-size: 20pt; white-space: pre-wrap;"><br /></span></p><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span style="font-size: 20pt; white-space: pre-wrap;">Interpreting: Never stop asking questions</span></p><p dir="ltr" style="line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 0pt; margin-top: 0pt;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">While many have moved on from ‘data-driven’ to ‘AI-enabled’, the fact remains that ALL AI SYSTEMS DEPEND ON </span><a href="https://hackernoon.com/the-ai-hierarchy-of-needs-18f111fcc007" style="text-decoration: none;"><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="color: #1155cc; font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; text-decoration-skip-ink: none; text-decoration: underline; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">DATA</span></a><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;">. Our data about open source will continue to be incomplete and imperfect, but by asking questions about our sources, acknowledging the gaps, and considering both the technical and human processes behind open source development, we can refine and improve on how we interpret our insights and models even if they don’t completely reflect reality.</span></p><div><span face="Arial, sans-serif" style="font-size: 11pt; font-variant: normal; vertical-align: baseline; white-space: pre-wrap;"><br /></span></div></span></description><link>https://opensource.googleblog.com/2026/09/how-much-should-you-trust-your-oss-data.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (KD)</author><media:thumbnail xmlns:media="http://search.yahoo.com/mrss/" url="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEhWI1EZBXgBioSYJ4vwVDAv5EZxIsFj7tna-3C-FSrZ5d-eCgOQIj97eycf_kjPnZW7JfRZyfYdbf6Wai8yIQEotI8pAbCkaxYREItO_MrZeZoNmweU2n42AXxTx4gZdRTThCuL4V6iyEnVU3hPx1BKn14hzP2Ro3rOHt4FL7ZFCH8zTaq_v1N2wPoSmb-X=s72-c" height="72" width="72"/></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-8698702854482141883.post-4345096551142443451</guid><pubDate>Tue, 18 Aug 2026 18:30:00 +0000</pubDate><atom:updated>2026-08-18T11:30:00.185-07:00</atom:updated><category domain="http://www.blogger.com/atom/ns#">AI</category><category domain="http://www.blogger.com/atom/ns#">CEL</category><category domain="http://www.blogger.com/atom/ns#">Common Expression Language</category><category domain="http://www.blogger.com/atom/ns#">formal verification</category><category domain="http://www.blogger.com/atom/ns#">open source</category><category domain="http://www.blogger.com/atom/ns#">security</category><title>Securing the agentic era: Introducing formal verification for CEL</title><description><p class="byline">by <author>Sean Huh</author>, Common Expression Language Team</p>

<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhuKigzFt1kkyx3eqlthONlcc6yKytKeoDmT2ADbA8GpreYwX_3zW2faeNB1D7F-NImDReaJs0TKdTB-gJjzKxhKpUaEXJef-PU2gIAJEfSrmvoUrLiBcyfqcxBrfYkP2TKUSIsY9SnuFVIAWVr_zFoJhyphenhyphen-pg_7XTlpt1dvs_yCce1obzhNJJkIC2umV8A/s1600/Cel_FullColor_RGB_notype.png">
<img class="metadata" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhuKigzFt1kkyx3eqlthONlcc6yKytKeoDmT2ADbA8GpreYwX_3zW2faeNB1D7F-NImDReaJs0TKdTB-gJjzKxhKpUaEXJef-PU2gIAJEfSrmvoUrLiBcyfqcxBrfYkP2TKUSIsY9SnuFVIAWVr_zFoJhyphenhyphen-pg_7XTlpt1dvs_yCce1obzhNJJkIC2umV8A/s1600/Cel_FullColor_RGB_notype.png" alt="CEL Formal Verification header graphic">
<a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhuKigzFt1kkyx3eqlthONlcc6yKytKeoDmT2ADbA8GpreYwX_3zW2faeNB1D7F-NImDReaJs0TKdTB-gJjzKxhKpUaEXJef-PU2gIAJEfSrmvoUrLiBcyfqcxBrfYkP2TKUSIsY9SnuFVIAWVr_zFoJhyphenhyphen-pg_7XTlpt1dvs_yCce1obzhNJJkIC2umV8A/s1600/Cel_FullColor_RGB_notype.png" class="header-image"><img border="0" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhuKigzFt1kkyx3eqlthONlcc6yKytKeoDmT2ADbA8GpreYwX_3zW2faeNB1D7F-NImDReaJs0TKdTB-gJjzKxhKpUaEXJef-PU2gIAJEfSrmvoUrLiBcyfqcxBrfYkP2TKUSIsY9SnuFVIAWVr_zFoJhyphenhyphen-pg_7XTlpt1dvs_yCce1obzhNJJkIC2umV8A/s1600/Cel_FullColor_RGB_notype.png" alt="CEL Formal Verification header graphic"/></a>

<p>We are rapidly entering an era where AI agents can autonomously draft, refactor, and deploy policies that protect our users and our systems. But this velocity introduces a vital question: <em>How do we trust AI-generated policies?</em></p>

<p>Unit tests may fail to cover the infinite set of possible inputs that occur in production; thus, an AI agent that overfits its policy to existing tests may fail spectacularly in production. To secure automated policy authoring, we must combine heuristic testing with mathematical proofs.</p>

<p>We are thrilled to announce the Common Expression Language (<a href="https://cel.dev/">CEL</a>) <a href="https://github.com/cel-expr/cel-java/tree/main/verifier">Formal Verification Framework</a> is now available. Powered by the <a href="https://github.com/Z3Prover/z3">Z3 theorem prover</a>, this framework allows you to prove the correctness of your CEL expressions and policies, serving as the ultimate safety net for the agentic policy.</p>

<p>Automated reasoning definitively answers questions like:</p>

<ul>
  <li>“Is there any combination of inputs that allows an unapproved request into production?”</li>
  <li>“Are we absolutely certain this AI-refactored policy matches the original behavior?”</li>
  <li>“Can a bad actor manipulate this rule to force an evaluation error?”</li>
</ul>

<p>Formal verification establishes mathematical certainty across the infinite spectrum of inputs. Proven policies protect your users and system while giving auditors clear proof of compliance.</p>

<p>To see these capabilities in action, watch our video demonstrating how the CEL Verifier REPL catches subtle logic flaws in seconds:</p>

<h2>Proving rules from the ground up</h2>

<p>Getting started with formal verification doesn’t require learning complex architectures right away. You can evaluate simple standalone CEL expressions to catch edge cases that tests easily miss.</p>

<p><em>(Note: The examples below use our interactive REPL syntax—check out the <a href="https://github.com/cel-expr/cel-java/blob/main/verifier/tools/README.md">REPL documentation</a> to follow along!)</em></p>

<h3>1. Catching logic bugs in simple expressions (Equivalence)</h3>

<p>How do you guarantee a refactored rule behaves identically to the original? Suppose we have a policy that allows ports 80 or 443 in production. An agent might factor the <em>is_prod</em> check like so:</p>

<pre><code class="codebox textproto">equiv
  (is_prod &amp;&amp; port == 80) || (is_prod &amp;&amp; port == 443) 
  &lt;=&gt;
  is_prod &amp;&amp; port == 80 || port == 443</code></pre>

<p>Because logical AND has a higher operator precedence than OR, the verifier immediately flags <strong>Violated</strong>, and outputs the exact exploit: in a non-production environment (<em>is_prod = false</em>), the rule mistakenly allows port 443. Fixing the grouping parentheses returns <strong>Verified</strong>.</p>

<h3>2. Enforcing exhaustive guardrails (Validity)</h3>

<p>This capability scales directly to use cases like Kubernetes Validating Admission Policies. Suppose an engineer writes a guardrail expression that assumes every request will either be on a low port (under 80) or a high port (over 1024):</p>

<pre><code class="codebox textproto">valid request.port &gt; 1024 || request.port &lt;= 80</code></pre>

<p>When we check validity (whether an expression holds true for all inputs), the verifier exhaustively searches the entire integer space, flags <strong>Violated</strong>, and outputs the exact counterexample:</p>

<pre><code class="codebox textproto">[VIOLATED] Condition is not always true. Counterexample input:
  request.port = 81</code></pre>

<h3>3. Guaranteeing security invariants with CEL Policy</h3>

<p>While the verifier works perfectly with standalone CEL expressions, complex environments compose multiple rules and variables. Here, the <a href="https://github.com/cel-expr/cel-policy">CEL policy format</a> shines. Using <em>assume</em> and <em>assert</em> blocks, the verifier proves a mathematical implication: if the assumptions hold, the assertions must also hold.</p>

<pre><code class="codebox textproto">name: workload_admission
rule:
  variables:
    - is_admin: 'request.auth.claims.groups.exists(g, g == "admin")'
  match:
    # A subtle flaw introduced during authoring:
    - condition: 'request.is_privileged &amp;&amp; request.is_prod'
      output: 'true'
    - condition: 'variables.is_admin || request.has_approval'
      output: 'true'
    - output: 'false'
verification:
  invariants:
    - id: universal_no_unapproved_privileged_prod
      assume:
        - 'request.has_approval == false'
        - 'variables.is_admin == false'
      assert:
        - 'rule.result == false'</code></pre>

<p>The first condition admits privileged workloads into production without checking for approval or admin status. The verifier flags this and provides an example that exploits the issue:</p>

<pre><code class="codebox textproto">Invariant 'universal_no_unapproved_privileged_prod' violation detected. Counterexample input:
  request.is_privileged = true
  request.is_prod = true
  request.has_approval = false
  request.auth.claims.groups = []</code></pre>

<p>Assertions and assumptions define the boundaries of acceptable agent behavior, allowing developers to configure CI/CD pipelines to validate AI-generated changes simply and securely.</p>

<h2>Under the hood: High-fidelity mathematical modeling</h2>

<p>Translating a dynamic language into the <a href="https://smt.st/SAT_SMT_by_example.pdf">Satisfiability Modulo Theories</a> (SMT) domain requires immense engineering rigor to prevent the solver from hanging or hallucinating bugs. Our engine provides:</p>

<h3>Zero false positives via three-pass taint tracking</h3>

<p>Traditional verification tools are prone to “solver hallucinations”—reporting fake bugs when encountering custom domain-specific functions or external variables they don’t fully understand. To eliminate this noise, if a potential issue relies on an unmapped custom function, the verifier isolates and flags it as <strong>Inconclusive</strong> rather than breaking your CI pipeline with a false alarm. This guarantees every <strong>Violation</strong> report is a 100% real, reproducible bug.</p>

<h3>Deep structural extensionality</h3>

<p>The Formal Verification Framework offers configurable-depth <strong>bounded-model checking</strong> to prevent infinite loops within SMT quantifiers. These configurable limits allow you to control the cost of verification when analyzing deep structure equivalence in expressions like <code class="inline">[[1], [2]] == [[1], [2]]</code>.</p>

<h2>The mandatory bridge of trust</h2>

<p>In the agentic era, code writes code. Mathematical proof isn’t just a nice-to-have; it is the fundamental bridge of trust developers require to let AI operate autonomously in their most sensitive systems. Get started with the <a href="https://github.com/cel-expr/cel-java/tree/main/verifier">CEL Formal Verification Framework</a>, to take the next step toward a more secure agentic future today!</p>

<p>Let us know what you think—issues, pull requests, and feedback are always welcome!</p>

<p>Google is committed to advancing open source silicon innovation. We are excited to share that we have formally joined the OpenROAD Initiative (ORI), Inc. as a principal member. ORI is a nonprofit public benefit corporation dedicated to the open source electronic design automation (EDA) ecosystem. As part of this commitment, Aaron Cunningham has been appointed to the ORI Governing Board to represent Google and help drive the foundation’s strategic direction, financial sustainability, and technical stewardship.</p>

<h2>Driving long-term open source sustainability</h2>

<p>The OpenROAD Initiative’s mission is to advance and sustain the open source EDA ecosystem by fostering collaborative innovation across research, education, and industry—transforming ideas into silicon. Google’s membership aligns directly with ORI’s multi-year sustainability goals, supported by the US National Science Foundation’s (NSF) Pathways to Enable Open-Source Ecosystems (POSE) program.</p>

<p>With Google’s participation and membership commitment, ORI will continue to strengthen, grow, and sustain its open source ecosystem through key vectors:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Neutral Stewardship</strong>: Fostering transparent governance where no single company has outsized control over the code, ensuring the project remains inspectable, accessible, and community-driven.</li>
  <li><strong>Ecosystem Growth</strong>: Supporting open and reproducible silicon research, developing robust design flows, and hosting global design contests.</li>
  <li><strong>Workforce Development</strong>: Supporting global silicon skilling initiatives by expanding open source chip design curricula and collaborating with academic institutions and industrial training networks.</li>
  <li><strong>Technical Strengthening</strong>: Enhancing continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, expanding PDK enablement, and improving user experience.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Leadership perspectives</h2>

<p>“The OpenROAD Initiative is built on the vision of making chip design open and accessible to all—building a collaborative ecosystem driven by transparency and shared innovation,” said Andrew Kahng, board member of the OpenROAD Initiative. “Google’s deep commitment to open source software and hardware makes them an ideal partner. By joining at our highest membership tier, Google is helping to ensure that the open source EDA ecosystem has the stable, long-term governance and financial foundation required to grow.”</p>

<p>“Cutting-edge silicon research requires robust, inspectable, and reproducible toolchains,” said Drew Wingard, Director of Silicon Infrastructure, Tools and Methodology at Google. “OpenROAD has already made an incredible impact across academia and the broader industry, enabling many successful tapeouts. Google is proud to support the OpenROAD Initiative’s mission to scale this open infrastructure for the next generation of developers.”</p>

<h2>About the OpenROAD Initiative and OpenROAD project</h2>

<p>The OpenROAD Initiative, Inc. is a California-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that provides governance, stewardship, and coordination for the OpenROAD ecosystem. The OpenROAD Project is an open source, autonomous digital chip design toolchain that democratizes semiconductor design, enabling a complete RTL-to-GDSII flow in less than 24 hours with no human in the loop. Grounded in academic research and referenced in over 500 peer-reviewed publications, OpenROAD has lowered the barriers to hardware innovation, enabling thousands of students, researchers, and startups worldwide to design and manufacture chips.</p>

<p>To learn more about the OpenROAD Project and install the toolchain, visit the new <a href="https://www.openroad.org">OpenROAD website</a>.</p>

<p>For more information about membership tiers and the foundation’s governance, visit the OpenROAD Initiative website at <a href="https://www.openroadinitiative.org">www.openroadinitiative.org</a> or contact <a href="mailto:membership@openroadinitiative.org">membership@openroadinitiative.org</a>.</p>

<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-developer-goog-blog-assets/images/image1_yEPzdSr.original.png">
<img class="metadata" src="https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-developer-goog-blog-assets/images/image1_yEPzdSr.original.png">

<p>Even as AI adoption accelerates and transforms the global technology landscape, open source remains foundational to how Alphabet builds, uses, and collaborates on products for billions of users. Our commitment to open source remains broad and consistent, including sharing our work year-over-year, and reflecting on what we've learned.</p>

<p>In 2025:</p>
<ul>
  <li>Roughly 10% of Alphabet's full-time workforce actively contributed to open source projects. This contribution ratio has remained steady over the past five years, scaling to match our growth.</li>
  <li>These open source contributions are not just solely focused on Google. Our top projects by unique contributors at Alphabet include community-led projects such as LLVM, vLLM, Envoy, and Rust, as well as Google-initiated projects like Kubernetes, Apache Beam, and gRPC.</li>
  <li>In addition, Alphabet projects <em>received</em> commits from more than 20,000 non-Alphabet affiliated user accounts.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Working together on emerging standards</h2>

<p>Open source communities continue to provide vital collaborative spaces to define emerging standards, ensuring the interoperability and extensibility for the next generation of technologies. In 2025, we worked with more than <a href="https://developers.googleblog.com/en/a2a-a-new-era-of-agent-interoperability/">50 partners on the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol</a> to enable AI agents to communicate with each other, securely exchange information, and coordinate actions on top of various enterprise platforms and applications. Within weeks of our initial announcement, <a href="https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-launches-the-agent2agent-protocol-project-to-enable-secure-intelligent-communication-between-ai-agents">Google donated the A2A project to the Linux Foundation</a> as part of our long-standing commitment to develop "open, collaborative ecosystem &ndash; offering greater autonomy and multiplying productivity."</p>

<figure class="wide borderless">
  <a href="https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-developer-goog-blog-assets/images/image1_yEPzdSr.original.png"><img alt="Google Cloud - Partners contributing to the Agent 2 Agent protocol - Accenture, Arize, Articul, ask-ai, Atlassian, BCG, Box, c3.ai, Capgemini, Chronosphere, Cognizant, Cohere, Colibra, Contextual.ai, Cotality, Datadog, and more" src="https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-developer-goog-blog-assets/images/image1_yEPzdSr.original.png"></a>
</figure>


<h2>Launching tools with transparency</h2>

<p>Open source licenses provide a framework for anyone to explore, test, fork and expand on our technologies. Over the last 15 years, Google has created more than 15,000 public repositories on GitHub. Today, Google continues to maintain more than 5,000 public repositories on GitHub, and more than 1,500 public repositories on Git-on-Borg. A quick look back to some highlights from our 2025 launches includes:</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/gemma-3/">Gemma 3</a> &ndash; a collection of lightweight <a href="https://opensource.googleblog.com/2024/02/building-open-models-responsibly-gemini-era.html">open models</a> built from the same research and technology that powers our Gemini 2.0 models. They are designed to run directly on devices &mdash; from phones and laptops to workstations &mdash; helping developers create AI applications, wherever people need them. Since Gemma&rsquo;s release in 2024, the <a href="https://deepmind.google/models/gemma/gemmaverse/">Gemmaverse</a> community has created more than 60,000 Gemma variants. We&rsquo;ve continued work on this collection and in 2026 we released <a href="https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/gemma-4/">Gemma 4</a> under an Apache 2.0 license.</li>
  <li><a href="https://developers.googleblog.com/en/agent-development-kit-easy-to-build-multi-agent-applications/">Agent Development Kit</a> &ndash; an open-source framework and SDK designed to help developers build, compose, and run both conversational and non-conversational AI agents.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Adjusting our collective security practices</h2>

<p>As the threat landscape evolves and accelerates in the AI era, we are working on novel solutions to mitigate vulnerabilities at scale and remove some of the burden from overloaded maintainers. In 2025, we introduced several critical security initiatives to support upstream open source projects:</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://deepmind.google/blog/introducing-codemender-an-ai-agent-for-code-security/"><strong>CodeMender</strong></a>: An agent designed to be both reactive, instantly patching new vulnerabilities, and proactive, rewriting and securing existing code and eliminating entire classes of vulnerabilities in the process. In its first six months, we were able to upstream 72 security fixes to open source projects, including some as large as 4.5 million lines of code.</li>
  <li><a href="https://blog.google/security/introducing-oss-rebuild-open-source/"><strong>OSS Rebuild</strong></a>: A security initiative to prevent software supply chain attacks by verifying build provenance. It automates package rebuilding and semantically compares results to upstream artifacts to detect tampered code on registries like PyPI, npm, and <a href="http://Crates.io">Crates.io</a>.</li>
  <li><a href="https://blog.google/security/announcing-osv-scanner-v2-vulnerability/"><strong>OSV-Scalibr</strong></a>: (Software Composition Analysis Library) the <a href="https://github.com/google/osv-scalibr">core engine</a> for vulnerability scanning used internally and in OSV-Scanner.</li>
  <li><a href="https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/securing-open-source-credentials-at-scale?e=0"><strong>Credential Scanning on deps.dev</strong></a>: A service (using <a href="https://opensource.googleblog.com/2025/07/stop-leaked-credentials-in-their-tracks-with-veles-our-new-open-source-secret-scanner.html">Veles</a>) that actively scans open-source packages on <a href="http://deps.dev/">deps.dev</a> for leaked GCP credentials to prevent account compromise.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Working together to sustain the contributor community</h2>

<p>Beyond security contributions, we remain committed to providing financial support directly to projects and maintainers. In 2025, the Open Source Programs Office (OSPO) directed $2M in sponsorships and investments to more than 40 open source projects.</p>

<p><a href="https://opensource.googleblog.com/2025/08/google-summer-of-code-2025-contributor-statistics.html">Google Summer of Code celebrated its 21st year</a> of enabling open source organizations to find, mentor, and onboard new contributors, directly supporting 1,280 individuals to contribute to 185 organizations. Over its lifetime, the global program has connected more than 23,000 participants from 125 countries with over 1,000 open source organizations globally. Moving forward, we recognize the need to evolve our program structures to ensure they continue to effectively support maintainers in the AI era.</p>

<h2>Evolving the way we work in open spaces</h2>

<p>Respecting community norms and practices is fundamental to establishing and maintaining trust in open source communities. To ensure we remain supportive members of your community, we encourage projects to document preferred practices and policies in the wake of new technologies. As AI changes the way we work, we are continually evaluating how best to <a href="https://opensource.googleblog.com/2026/06/community-feedback-how-can-corporations-improve-support-for-open-source-maintainers.html">evolve the way we engage</a> in open spaces to preserve, prepare and bolster the communities we depend on.</p>

<p>We are deeply grateful for the many individuals and organizations that have worked with us to create global technologies from which <em>everyone</em> can benefit. You can continue to learn more about our open source initiatives, ongoing programs, and new projects at <a href="https://opensource.google">opensource.google</a>.</p>

<h2>Appendix: About this data</h2>

<p>This report features metrics provided by many teams and programs across Alphabet. In regards to the code and code-adjacent activities data, we wanted to share more details about the derivation of those metrics.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Data sources:</strong> These data represent the activities of Alphabet employees on public repositories hosted on GitHub and our internal production Git service <a href="https://opensource.google/documentation/reference/glossary#git-on-borg">Git-on-Borg</a>. These sources represent a subset of open source activity currently tracked by Google OSPO.</li>
  <li><strong>Business and personal:</strong> Activity on GitHub reflects a mixture of Alphabet projects, third-party projects, experimental efforts, and personal projects. Our metrics report on all of the above unless otherwise specified.</li>
  <li><strong>Alphabet contributors:</strong> Please note that unless additional detail is specified, activity counts attributed to Alphabet open source contributors will include our full-time employees as well as our extended Alphabet community (temps, vendors, contractors, and interns). In 2025, full time employees at Alphabet represented more than 95% of our open source contributors.</li>
  <li><strong>GitHub Accounts:</strong> For counts of GitHub accounts not affiliated with Alphabet, we cannot assume that one account is equivalent to one person, as multiple accounts could be tied to one individual or bot account.</li>
  <li><strong>Active counts:</strong> Where possible, we will show &lsquo;active users&rsquo; defined by logged activity (excluding &lsquo;WatchEvent&rsquo;) within a specified timeframe (a month, year, etc.) and &lsquo;active repositories&rsquo; and &lsquo;active projects&rsquo; as those that have enough activity to meet our internal active-project criteria and have not been archived.</li>
</ul>

<h2>This Week in Open Source for July 16, 2026</h2>
<p>A look around the world of open source</p>

<p>We’re diving into another week of open source news and discussions. As the ecosystem continues to evolve, we're seeing more conversations around the intersection of AI workflows, security at scale, and the infrastructure that supports the open web.</p>

<p>This week, we’re highlighting a few "Open Source Reads" that tackle some of the biggest questions facing our ecosystem today—from the complex ethics of AI-generated workflows to the future of federated social networks. We hope these links provide valuable context as we work together to sustain the critical infrastructure we all rely on.</p>

<h2>Upcoming Events</h2>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://events.linuxfoundation.org/open-source-days/">ASWF Open Source Days</a> (July 19–20) — Los Angeles, CA. Hosted by the <a href="https://www.aswf.io/">Academy Software Foundation</a>, focusing on open source software in visual effects (VFX) and animation.</li>
<li><a href="https://events.linuxfoundation.org/kubecon-cloudnativecon-japan/">KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Japan 2026</a> (July 28–30) — Yokohama, Japan. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation's flagship conference in Japan.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.blackhat.com/">Black Hat</a> &amp; <a href="https://defcon.org/">DEF CON 2026</a> (August 1–9) — Las Vegas, NV. While primarily cybersecurity, both heavily feature open source hacking tools. The Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) also has a major presence here.</li>
<li><a href="https://2026.fossy.ca/">FOSSY</a> (August 6–9) — Vancouver, Canada. A highly community-focused open source conference emphasizing grassroots participation and collaboration.</li>
<li><a href="https://asia.communityovercode.org/">Community over Code Asia</a> (August 7–9) — Beijing, China. The Asian edition of the Apache Software Foundation's (ASF) community-first conference.</li>
<li><a href="https://events.linuxfoundation.org/open-source-summit-korea/">Open Source Summit Korea</a> (August 11–12) — Seoul, South Korea. Hosted by the Linux Foundation, bringing together open source maintainers and enterprises.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.lfasiallc.com/kubecon-cloudnativecon-openinfra-summit-pytorch-conference-china/">KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China</a> (September 7–9) — Shanghai, China. A massive collaborative mega-event uniting open infrastructure, cloud, and AI communities.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.lfopensource.cn/kubecon-cloudnativecon-openinfra-summit-pytorch-conference-china/co-located-events/ospology-ospo-summit/">OSPOlogy + OSPO Summit</a> (September 7) — Shanghai, China. Focused on Open Source Program Offices (OSPOs), governance, and corporate open source sustainability.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Open Source Reads and Links</h2>
<ul>
<li>[Blog] <a href="https://drensin.medium.com/elephants-goldfish-and-the-new-golden-age-of-software-engineering-c33641a48874">Elephants, Goldfish and the New Golden Age of Software Engineering</a> - This isn't directly open source, but with the open source ecosystem trying to find good AI workflows I thought the Elephant-Goldfish model was an interesting take. It makes the distinction between using AI as a toy and using it as a tool.</li>
<li>[Article] <a href="https://unu.edu/article/open-source-ai-and-the-choice-before-us">Open-source AI and the Choice Before Us</a> - The communities with minimal influence on AI development will likely be the most affected by it. This article looks at how strong rules and institutions are needed to guide AI's safe and fair use. The future of AI depends on whether we build systems that include everyone or just deepen existing divides.</li>
<li>[Article] <a href="https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/mythos-zero-day-patches-project-akrites">Open source carries the world. Patching it at Mythos-scale can't fall to maintainers alone.</a> - The past year has shown that AI is speeding up the discovery of vulnerabilities in open source software. Endor Labs is offering a solution to utilize AI to create patching stop gaps for users of the libraries so that maintainers and contributors have the time to create good quality fixes to these vulnerabilities.</li>
<li>[Blog] <a href="https://bnewbold.leaflet.pub/3mph4hzvbdc2v">The AT-URI Syntax Mess</a> - I am very excited about the open social web, especially things happening around the AT protocol. Early misunderstanding led to the current AT URI syntax being invalid. This article looks at the possible ways forward.</li>
<li>[Article] <a href="https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/04/open-social-web-needs-section-230-survive">The Open Social Web Needs Section 230 to Survive</a> - The open web has always been a promise of free speech. When walled garden social media got involved it created some questions around whether free speech applies to the content served by the corporations running those networks. However, the open social web is not run by corporations. It can be, and it can also be run by individuals federating instances or running their own PDS. So, how do we maintain the free speech promise of the internet with this in mind?</li>
</ul>

<p>We know that AI is actively <a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.04921">transforming</a> the sustainability and socio-technical dynamics of OSS communities. Google Open Source is committed to partnering with open source communities and ecosystems to learn together how we should update our own models for engagement and support.</p>

<p>During an open meetup for <a href="https://maintainermonth.github.com/">GitHub Maintainer Month</a>, I led a session to gather community feedback on how corporations can more effectively support open source maintainers.</p>

<h2>Paying maintainers takes creativity</h2>
<p>Many maintainers would appreciate consistent financial support. However, facilitating payments to individuals without established contractual relationships remains a complex challenge, particularly across diverse international jurisdictions. Fiscal hosts and programs such as <a href="https://opencollective.com/">Open Collective</a>, <a href="https://github.com/open-source/sponsors">GitHub Sponsors</a>, and the <a href="https://lfx.linuxfoundation.org/tools/mentorship/">LFX Mentorship Program</a> can simplify components of this process, but they do not resolve the underlying issues of funding sustainability and predictability. While initiatives like the <a href="https://endowment.dev/">Open Source Endowment</a> are working toward long-term funding sustainability, individual maintainers also had a few ideas:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Pay per meaningful contribution vs gameable metrics: </strong>Avoid payment models based on easily manipulated units like pull request counts or review volume. A proposed alternative is <strong>‘pay per report,'</strong> encouraging maintainers to document their achievements and upcoming roadmaps.</li>
<li><strong>Commitment-based purchasing: </strong>Corporate policies might make procurement simpler (or more complex) than sponsorships, so maintainers could benefit from offering structured support services alongside traditional sponsorship opportunities.</li>
<li><strong>Fund conference attendance: </strong>In-person networking can be a boon for solo maintainers but it's often cost-prohibitive. For some corporations, travel sponsorship may be a simpler alternative to direct payments.</li>
</ul>

<table class="style0">
    <tr>
      <td class="style1"><em><strong>Challenge for Corporations and Fiscal Hosts</strong>:</em> How can we assist maintainers in understanding any and all prerequisites and documentation necessary to participate in monetary programs?</td>
      <td class="style2"><em><strong>Advice from Maintainers</strong></em>: Consult a tax professional to understand the implications of various funding methods.</td>
    </tr>
</table>

<h2>Manage and respect expectations</h2>
<p>Beyond financial support, our discussion returned to the importance of respect and etiquette. Particularly, how can we manage expectations between heterogeneous creators, contributors and users -<strong> </strong>are maintainers clearly communicating their preferences, and are corporations actively respecting them? Some suggestions include:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Adherence to community norms: </strong>Maintainers should share their preferred communication channels, while contributors - both human and agentic - must ensure they review and follow them.</li>
<li><strong>Consistency with documentation: </strong>Discrepancies between documented procedures and actual practices create friction for all participants. This standard should be upheld by both individual maintainers and corporate-managed projects.</li>
<li><strong>Clarity of intent: </strong>Many maintainers would like to understand the motivation behind a contribution and reserve the right to ask questions.</li>
</ul>

<p>To improve specific program experiences, maintainers suggested:</p>

<ul>
<li><strong>Consistent communication: </strong>Recipients of funding programs expect clearly communicated expectations regarding the timing and amount of disbursements.</li>
<li><strong>Transparency and discoverability: </strong>Maintainers would appreciate easily discoverable records that track program participation, active agreements, and verify the status of Contributor License Agreements (CLAs).</li>
</ul>

<h2>Let's keep learning as a community</h2>
<p>While we cannot make any promises, we want to continue to learn and challenge ourselves to consider novel ways to support OSS communities and maintainers. As a member of our community, we value your opinion. We've created a <a href="https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScb2EC-DcmJ1OdK-Zw5cCirvnelCGWdrN-vQtfXnYIQA1wgTQ/viewform?usp=header">Google form</a> to collect any thoughts you might have, as well as gauge interest in another open meeting. We plan to share any and all learnings back with the community.</p>

<p>When you think of "innovation" in open source, your mind probably jumps to the latest AI model or a revolutionary new framework. You might not immediately think of manual pages. Even Alejandro "Alex" Colomar, who spends his days <a href="https://www.kernel.org/doc/man-pages/maintaining.html">maintaining Linux Kernel documentation</a>, jokingly admits that some might find the work "boring" because it focuses on fixing existing issues and documenting new features rather than flashy inventions.</p><p>
But as any developer knows, the most powerful code is only as good as the documentation behind it. At Google, we believe that investing in the success of projects we don't own is a core part of being a good open source citizen. That is why we are proud to <a href="https://www.linux.com/news/celebrating-the-second-year-of-linux-man-pages-maintenance-sponsorship/">sponsor Alejandro's work</a> on the Linux Kernel man-pages project—supporting the critical infrastructure that many of our own systems rely on every day.</p>
<blockquote>Documentation is the gift you give to your future self and your whole community.</blockquote>

<h2>The precision of a robot</h2>
<p>Alejandro's journey into the world of essential documentation started at university. He was working with robotic arms that used a proprietary scripting language. Wanting more control, he decided to write a C library to communicate with the robots over the network by sniffing packets with Wireshark. It worked, but it was slow—he had to wait seconds between commands to ensure the robot had finished moving.</p>
<p>To make the movements smooth, he needed to understand the messages the robot was sending back in real-time. This required high-precision timing. He found <code class="inline">SO_TIMESTAMP</code>, which provided microsecond precision, but he noticed a macro called <code class="inline">SO_TIMESTAMPNS</code> in the header files that promised nanosecond resolution. The problem? It wasn't documented in the manual page.</p>

<h2>The first patch</h2>
<p>After figuring out how to use the undocumented feature by looking at the kernel source code, Alejandro decided to ensure the next person wouldn't have to struggle. He cloned the man-pages repository, wrote a new paragraph based on existing features, and figured out how to send a plain-text patch via email.</p><p>
"As it was my first patch, I was a bit intimidated by the procedure," Alejandro recalls. That intimidation led to a commit message he is still proud of today: roughly 120 lines of explanation for just 25 lines of new documentation. He wanted to prove that he had done his homework. The welcoming response from the maintainer encouraged him to keep going, leading to more patches and, eventually, a career-long dedication to clarity in open source communities.</p>

<h2>Sustaining the commons</h2>
<p>Google understands that open source is a "small community built on trust." By supporting maintainers like Alejandro, we help ensure that critical infrastructure—like the documentation that powers the Linux ecosystem—remains accurate and accessible for everyone. We believe that using open source comes with a responsibility to contribute and sustain it, which is why we partner with developers to maintain and grow critical projects.</p><p>
Alejandro's work doesn't just help himself; it helps thousands of other programmers who rely on correct documentation to build the next generation of technology. As he puts it: "I couldn't program without correct documentation, so whenever I find an issue in documentation, I try to fix it."</p>

<h2>A garden that needs tending</h2>
<p>We often say that a community is a garden, not a building—it requires constant tending, not just initial construction. By sponsoring Alejandro, we are helping to tend that garden, ensuring the "manual" remains a living, breathing resource for the global developer ecosystem. Whether it is fixing a typo or documenting a high-precision networking macro, every contribution makes the "eyes" on the code that much sharper.</p></description><link>https://opensource.googleblog.com/2026/06/documenting-the-manual-how-curiosity-and-robotic-arms-led-to-a-career-in-open-source.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Google Open Source)</author><media:thumbnail xmlns:media="http://search.yahoo.com/mrss/" url="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgwzJszSMRbAj7eM_f4aXx0OqZW72VjPDjvgV7ew9WiCUvUgdFtqunL5ySeShN7KD_eCNFlYdJY6gDRMjLmC7CzSriHzAHwEdwyOYdbmN2T6GyLf8mgI3OHcY4e9vpsPe6AE_t5lbw3E5cdV91M78Z83vRFHL3Ny_wiGTDJsrPGkKPZ6cco0wwlWhaLt-8/s72-c/OSS-Logo-Banner.png" height="72" width="72"/></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-8698702854482141883.post-1393140882587930163</guid><pubDate>Thu, 18 Jun 2026 18:30:00 +0000</pubDate><atom:updated>2026-06-18T11:30:00.113-07:00</atom:updated><category domain="http://www.blogger.com/atom/ns#">AI</category><category domain="http://www.blogger.com/atom/ns#">Kubernetes</category><category domain="http://www.blogger.com/atom/ns#">ML</category><title>In-place pod restarts: Boosting efficiency and workload reliability in Kubernetes v1.35</title><description><p class="byline">by <author>Duncan Campbell</author> &amp; <author>Giuseppe Tinti Tomio</author>, Kubernetes</p>

<p>Operational efficiency and system resilience are critical when running scaled platforms. Yet, in Kubernetes, recovering from software crashes remains a headache because you couldn't trigger a clean restart of a Pod's containers without recreating the entire Pod object, leading to some amount of resource waste.<br>
To address this, <strong>Restart All Containers on Container Exits</strong> graduated to beta and is enabled by default in Kubernetes v1.36. Developed in close collaboration with the CNCF community, this capability represents Google's commitment to investing in the success of foundation-led open source projects. By sharing best practices from running large distributed systems internally, we are helping build a more resilient and efficient ecosystem. Letting containers restart while keeping the Pod's runtime identity provides a built-in way to perform in-place Pod recovery, boosting application reliability and saving resource costs.</p>

<h2>The Problem: The High Cost of Pod Re-creation</h2>
<p>Historically, Kubernetes managed failures using pod level restart policies. While sufficient for simple services, modern multi-container Pods often have complex dependencies. When a failure requires a full environment reset, your only option was deleting and recreating the entire Pod.<br>
This introduces massive control plane churn, causing latency and pressure on the etcd backend during large failures:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Initialization Dependencies:</strong> If a main container corrupts a local environment, for example, single-use secrets that must be re-requested, restarting just that container is insufficient; the setup must run again.</li>
<li><strong>Watcher Interoperability:</strong> If a watcher sidecar detects a fatal error, it must trigger a full recreate of the entire pod and its infrastructure, including the sandbox.</li>
<li><strong>Stale States:</strong> If a database sidecar proxy restarts, the main application can get stuck attempting to use stale, broken connections.</li>
<li><strong>Resource Race Conditions:</strong> When a large job finds a proper set of nodes, recreating Pods can lead to other pending Pods taking over those resources. In-place restarts eliminate this race condition risk.</li>
</ul>
<p>Previously, resolving these failures required destroying the entire Pod. For large batch or AI/ML workloads, where thousands of Pods might fail simultaneously, this can lead to "Thundering Herd" scheduling requests, delaying recovery and wasting expensive GPU/TPU compute time.</p>

<h2>Introducing In-Place Restarts: The RestartAllContainers Action</h2>
<p>Kubernetes v1.35 introduces the <code>RestartAllContainers</code> action, enabled by the <code>RestartAllContainersOnContainerExits</code> feature gate, which graduated to beta in 1.36 alongside its dependencies <code>ContainerRestartRules</code> and <code>NodeDeclaredFeatures</code>. This lets a container's exit behavior trigger a fast, in-place restart of the entire Pod on its existing node.<br>
The Kubelet halts all containers while keeping the Pod sandbox intact, preserving critical infrastructure:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Network Identity:</strong> Keeps the same IP, network namespace, and UID, completely bypassing IP reassignment.</li>
<li><strong>Hardware and Devices:</strong> Keeps GPUs/TPUs bound, eliminating scheduling and re-allocation delays.</li>
<li><strong>Storage Mounts:</strong> Volumes, including <code>emptyDir</code> and PVCs, remain fully mounted; their content is not cleared during restarts.</li>
</ul>
<p>Once terminated, the Kubelet re-runs init containers (including sidecars, which are part of the init sequence) in order, guaranteeing a clean setup in a known-good environment.</p>

<h3>A Native Pod Specification Example</h3>
<p>You can implement this under the container's <code>restartPolicyRules</code> field. Here is a quick example of how a watcher sidecar can trigger an in-place restart of the entire Pod by exiting with code 88:<br>
YAML<br>
<em>Note: Image names and paths in the YAML below are for illustrative purposes.</em></p>

<pre><code class="codebox yaml">apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: ml-worker-pod
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  initContainers:
    - name: setup-environment
      image: registry.k8s.io/ml-tools/setup-worker:v1.0
    - name: watcher-sidecar
      image: registry.k8s.io/ml-tools/watcher:v1.0
      restartPolicy: Always
      restartPolicyRules:
        - action: RestartAllContainers
          exitCodes:
            operator: In
            values: [88]
  containers:
    - name: main-application
      image: registry.k8s.io/ml-tools/training-app:v1.0</code></pre>

<h2>The Operational Impact of In-Place Restarts</h2>
<p>For organizations running distributed workloads, <code>RestartAllContainers</code> provides serious operational advantages:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>No Control Plane Overhead:</strong> By preserving identity, clusters avoid scheduling latency and DNS propagation. This was a key factor for JobSet using this feature to reduce recovery from minutes to seconds.</li>
<li><strong>Node Locality Preservation:</strong> Since the Pod stays anchored to the same node, restarted containers can instantly access local, warm storage caches.</li>
<li><strong>Maximized Hardware Efficiency:</strong> In distributed AI training, losing a single node halts the entire job. Keeping accelerators like GPUs/TPUs bound lets workloads resume training significantly faster, directly reducing compute costs.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Observability and SRE Best Practices</h2>
<p>To support monitoring, Kubernetes v1.35 introduces the <code>AllContainersRestarting</code> Pod condition. Set to <code>True</code> during restarts, it alerts SREs and autoscalers, preventing false-positive alerts, while container restart counts increment to let Prometheus easily track recovery events.<br>
To use in-place restarts successfully, shift your mental model to "persistent sandboxes" and follow three best practices:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Ensure Reentrancy:</strong> Kubelet only guarantees "at least once" execution for init containers. Reentrancy is now a standard requirement, so your code must be fully idempotent.</li>
<li><strong>Plan for Termination Handling:</strong> Graceful termination (<code>preStop</code> hooks) is not supported for in-place restarts. SIGKILL is almost immediate, so applications must handle sudden exits gracefully.</li>
<li><strong>Prepare External Tooling:</strong> CD and observability tools should expect re-running init containers without interpreting them as new deployments.</li>
</ol>

<h2>What's Next?</h2>
<p>This beta capability is a major step toward fluid workload management and serves as a building block for advanced community features like JobSet in-place restarts <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/issues/467">(KEP-467)</a>.<br>
Our work on KEP-5532 reflects our commitment to transparent open source governance. Developed collaboratively within SIG Node, this feature shows how we hold ourselves to high citizenship standards; making our design, goals, and intentions transparent while building shared best practices that benefit everyone. We encourage you to experiment with Kubernetes v1.35 and share your feedback with the community!</p>

<p>At Open Source Summit North America 2026, I shared why agentic commerce needs open rails.</p>

<p>As AI agents become more capable, the shopping journey is shifting from "show me" to "help me." Instead of browsing, comparing, clicking, and checking out step by step, people can increasingly ask an agent to help them decide what to buy and, in some cases, complete the purchase. Industry forecasts suggest agentic shopping could account for roughly 10% to 25% of U.S. e-commerce by 2030 (<a href="https://www.bain.com/insights/2030-forecast-how-agentic-ai-will-reshape-us-retail-snap-chart/?utm_source=chatgpt.com">Bain</a>), which points to a meaningful shift in how digital commerce will work. Watch the full keynote <a href="https://youtu.be/FmrJNTqRTVM?si=Kh2M0TKBv8uRZc6a">here</a>.</p>

<h2>Why shared rules matter</h2>

<p>That shift also exposes a challenge. Commerce is still highly fragmented. Different businesses, payment providers, and platforms operate with their own rules, workflows, and business logic. Every new surface adds more integration work. Every bespoke connection creates more complexity. And that fragmentation makes it harder for AI systems to understand and perform commerce actions consistently across businesses. A shared language lowers that barrier for everyone.</p>

<p><strong>A common language for agentic commerce</strong></p>

<p>That is the problem <a href="https://ucp.dev/">Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP)</a>  is designed to solve.</p>

<p>We launched the Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP, with industry leaders to establish an open standard for agentic commerce, built to work across the shopping journey. UCP creates a common language for agents and systems to operate together across consumer surfaces, businesses, and payment providers, so the ecosystem does not need a different bespoke integration for every new agent or platform.</p>

<p>Just as importantly, UCP is designed for the real world. Every business has its own way of selling. Checkout, fulfillment, loyalty, policy logic, shipping, and post-purchase flows can vary widely between a local shop, a marketplace, and a large retailer. UCP is built to support that reality.</p>

<h2>A layered architecture for a shared commerce language</h2>

<p>UCP uses a layered model to create a reusable shared language for commerce. <strong>Services</strong> organize domains like shopping and common. <strong>Capabilities</strong> define core actions such as checkout, catalog, cart, orders, and shared functions like identity linking. <strong>Extensions</strong> keep those capabilities configurable, so features like fulfillment can be modeled once and reused across multiple flows instead of being hardwired each time. At the <strong>transport</strong> layer, UCP stays agnostic, supporting bindings like REST, Model Context Protocol, and Agent2Agent.</p>

<p>Together with capability discovery and payment handling, these layers help consumer platforms, agents, and businesses interoperate more consistently over time. They also let different participants advertise what they support, compose new behaviors, and communicate over the transport that works best for them.</p>

<h2>Built in the open</h2>

<p>A standard for everyone should be shaped by everyone. Because UCP is open, merchants, developers, and community contributors can pressure-test real-world gaps, propose new capabilities and extensions, and help make sure the protocol reflects more than the needs of the largest players. That kind of participation is what keeps an ecosystem moving.</p>

<p>Since launch, UCP has continued to evolve through <a href="https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/shopping/ucp-updates/">new capabilities</a>, an <a href="https://github.com/Universal-Commerce-Protocol/ucp/discussions/379">expanded Tech Council</a>, and <a href="https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/shopping/google-shopping-cart/">new consumer experiences</a> built on top of the protocol. That momentum matters because standards only work when the ecosystem uses them.</p>

<p>Agentic commerce is still evolving, and UCP is a foundational building block to support what's next in this new era.</p>

<p>We're excited to announce that the official Common Expression Language (CEL) repositories have moved to a dedicated GitHub organization. Visit the new<a href="https://github.com/cel-expr"> cel-expr repository</a> now!</p><p>
<h2>Why the move?</h2>
<p>This move is a key step in strengthening the CEL ecosystem. By centralizing our projects, including the language specification, Go, C++, C, Java, and Python implementations, under the <code>cel-expr</code> organization, we aim to:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Enhance Branding:</strong> Create a clear and unified brand identity for CEL.</li>
<li><strong>Improve Discoverability:</strong> Make it easier for users and contributors to find all official CEL resources in one place.</li>
<li><strong>Ensure Consistency:</strong> Foster consistency across all CEL projects.</li>
<li><strong>Streamline Development:</strong> Simplify our development and release processes.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>What's Changing?</strong></p><p>
The following repositories now reside in the <code>cel-expr</code> organization:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>google/cel-spec</code> is now <code>cel-expr/cel-spec</code></li>
<li><code>google/cel-cpp</code> is now <code>cel-expr/cel-cpp</code></li>
<li><code>google/cel-go</code> is now <code>cel-expr/cel-go</code></li>
<li><code>google/cel-java</code> is now <code>cel-expr/cel-java</code></li>
  <li><code>cel-expr/cel-python</code> and <code>cel-expr/cel-c</code> have already been in the <code>cel-expr</code> namespace</li>
</ul>
<p>All future development, issues, and pull requests for these projects will take place in their new homes within the <code>cel-expr</code> organization. This is a non-breaking change, due to automatic redirects, but you should update your URLs where possible.</p><p>
<strong>What Stays the Same?</strong></p><p>
We've worked to make this transition as seamless as possible:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Automatic Redirects:</strong> GitHub will automatically redirect all web traffic and <code>git</code> operations from the old <code>google/cel-*</code> URLs to the new <code>cel-expr/cel-*</code> locations. Your existing links and <code>git remote</code> configurations pointing to the old URLs should continue to work for cloning and fetching.</li>
<li><strong>Preserved History:</strong> The full commit history, issues, and pull requests for each repository have been migrated and are available in the new locations.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Action Required: Update Your Dependencies</strong></p><p>
While existing links and <code>git remote</code> configurations pointing to the old URLs should continue to work thanks to GitHub's redirects, we recommend updating your dependency management configurations (e.g., <code>go.mod</code>, <code>pom.xml</code>, <code>requirements.txt</code>, etc.) to point directly to the new repository URLs under <code>https://github.com/cel-expr</code>. This ensures you are fetching the latest code and releases from the canonical source.</p><p>
We're thrilled about this new chapter for CEL, bringing all our core components under one roof. We believe this will foster a stronger CEL community and accelerate the development and adoption of CEL.</p><p>

<p>
Access to Go metadata has been an everpresent need for the Go community. Since its launch, <a href="http://pkg.go.dev">pkg.go.dev</a> has served as a central hub for Go package documentation and discovery. While we initially prioritized providing this comprehensive access via a web interface, the need for streamlined programmatic access has become increasingly clear.
</p>
<p>
Structured API access has been one of the most highly requested features for <a href="http://pkg.go.dev">pkg.go.dev</a> for a while now. Developers building tools, IDE integrations, automated workflows, and other systems have had to rely on inconsistent and fragile scraping methods. By providing a formal API, we can provide fast and efficient access to required data. This foundation also sets Go up for the future of AI-assisted coding. Large language models and agents can access the context necessary to reason about the Go ecosystem with greater precision and accuracy. 
</p>
<h2>Empowering Tool Builders</h2>


<p>
Our goal with this API is to reduce the technical churn for builders and innovators. By offering structured JSON metadata, we address the following use cases:
</p>
<ul>

<li><strong>Search and Discovery: </strong>The API enables fast and efficient search across the entire Go module ecosystem.</li>

<li><strong>Driving AI Innovation:</strong> As AI-assisted coding evolves, LLMs and agents need precise context. This API provides the data required for agents and models to reason deterministically about Go packages.</li>
</ul>
<h2>The Service Interface</h2>


<p>
Built for stability and efficient caching, the API uses a stateless, GET-only architecture. Primary endpoints are currently hosted under the <code>v1beta</code> path. Following a period of feedback from the Go community and confirmed stability, we intend to transition toward a formal <code>v1</code> release.
</p>
<p>
For a complete interactive reference of all endpoints, query parameters, and
response shapes, see <a href="http://pkg.go.dev/api">pkg.go.dev/api</a>. The machine-readable API contract is also published directly at <a href="http://pkg.go.dev/v1beta/openapi.yaml">pkg.go.dev/v1beta/openapi.yaml</a>.
</p>
